I was part of the minority of players that enjoyed the game at launch, but this review is for the current state of the game as of 3/30/2021.

Do you yearn for exploration? When you play a new game, do you canvas the entire map looking for interesting things? Do you only get a dopamine rush from seeing something in a game that you have never seen before?

If you said yes to these questions, then this game is perfect for you.

The early game is a little rough, but once you get a decent amount of income, the game really opens up with the amount of things you are able to do.

My main gameplay tips:
- You should try to finish the first part of the main story as quickly as possible, because it opens up a lot of the other mechanics in the game.
- Get a lot of salvaged data and make a base with unlocked parts as soon as possible. Having a base will let you dig for deep mineral deposits or farm, which can quickly make you A LOT of money.
- Upgrade your scanner on your multitool with three S-class upgrades. Doing this, if you're lucky with the upgrade rolls, can mean that scanning a single new creature on a planet will give you ~500,000 units in one go.
- Try to mostly visit systems that have a three-star economy. You can buy and sell goods for better prices there, you will get more valuable ships there, and potentially more valuable multitools.
- Because this game can seem pointless if viewed from a big picture perspective, try to alternate what you do every time you play. One day you can set up a deep mineral extraction mine, the next day clear out some desolate freighters, the next day talk to a bunch of Korvax to fill out your lexicon, the next day fly around looking for a better ship, etc. This way you won't get bored, at least not until you hit 200+ hours.

I'll end by saying that this game is not for everyone. Hell, I take months-long breaks from it and return once in a while to try out new content and do some relaxing exploration. Overall it's a hell of a lot better than it was at launch, and one of the most interesting games I've ever played.

I don't think anybody would deny that Hello Games deserves utmost commendation for their phenomenal dedication towards building their game up to be more in line with what they promised; this being said, No Man's Sky yet still struggles not to be a shadow of what it truly could be. Exploration becomes stale and unexciting after the first system or two. Planets, fauna, and flora end up all acting and looking nearly identical, despite being hundreds of star systems apart. Base building is fun but entirely inefficient and unfulfilling aside from storing items. Economy is pointless and easily exploited. Ruins, wrecks, and distress signals are unrewarding and lack any substance aside from material gain. Star-ships suffer a similar plague to the animals and plants, being that they all end up looking, feeling, and doing the same thing but have a different color or cockpit style. They're fun to collect, but with lack of both cosmetic and non-cosmetic customization and personalization, it's frustrating to wade in such an in-depth concept when it's stuck at such a shallow level.

What should be a reward for the curiosity of the player instead becomes 300 credits for "discovering" the exact same flower you've seen on the last three planets but happens to be of a different name. Plainly, there just isn't enough variation to overcome its platitudinous nature. With procedural generation being the culprit and the core of NMS, it is hard to overlook how glaringly bland the "discovery" aspect of this game still remains, five years later. The updates that Hello Games has released within the last couple of years are definitely interesting and exciting; doubtless, they are good content. However, the problem lies with the fact that these updates are great DLC additions to an average game, which hinders you from enjoying the newer content to the fullest extent due to the underlying game being lackluster. A car with the most exotic, most thrilling, and most beautiful of body designs amounts to nothing if the engine is insipid and problematic. 

I have nothing but respect for Hello Games and their "actions>words" mentality and approach. Maybe one day, they will give No Man's Sky the deep rethinking that it desperately needs to achieve what they first envisioned. Until then though, aside from a decent and aesthetically pleasing time waster, I cannot recommend NMS if you're looking for the ultimate space exploration experience that we all believed it would be.

No Man's Sky, or: Beauty really only goes skin deep.

Look, I'm not going to rehash NMS' tragic origin story. If that's going to dissuade you from buying this game, you already know it. I'm going to be talking about NMS now, now that it actually is a complete game. 

I've invested a fair amount of time in to this title, giving it a truly fair shake every time it published an update, but honestly, now, I'm at the point where I know the story by heart. Hello Games announces an exciting new feature to the game that reinvigorates the user base. A flood of players flocks to the game to check it out, and some really cool screenshots come out of it. Then, the players like me who need depth and complexity to gameplay discover that the new feature is basically a *really* pretty wading pool. 

Take the new pets- they all pretty much serve the same purpose, so much so that unique pets on unique worlds can't be tamed, because they can't be ridden or given saddlebags. You can customize the aesthetic of pets, and they have a few stats you can try to breed for, and... well, that's it. You don't breed pets with other types of monsters, or even other parents of its own species- you just get eggs that more or less clone the exact parent. I saw the companions update, and I was picturing variants of various monsters walking around, but no, they're all carbon copy clones of each other in various sizes. *Pocket Frogs* had a better breeding system than this.

See, NMS is a game that seems to serve a single purpose- Coming up with cool screenshots. If that's your bag, NMS will have mountains of content for you. If you're a mechanically driven gamer, look elsewhere, friends.

Hello Games, give us a DEPTH update. Let us customize our exocraft with different exocraft parts that we craft. Let different varieties of the same monster roam the planet, and give us dual parent genetic breeding. Coding punnet squares is easy, I promise. Give us more weapon modules. And no, modules that just make numbers go up don't count. Give us things that *feel* different. Let us plant different varieties of trees and plants on our planets, to really make a world feel rich and diverse. Stop giving us new features, and start giving us DEPTH.

Good: Great visuals, good sound design, and a decent core gameplay loop make for at least 10 hours of solid gameplay,

Bad: The game can still be buggy in places, multiplayer doesn't really give you a feel of togetherness (communal base building, please...), and NMS' progression has more to do with difference in scale, rather than difference in kind.

Ugly: The aftermath of trying to dive in to a 1' deep wading pool.

The day is august 9th, 2016. One word is on the lips of all reviewers: dissapointed. No Man's Sky was a failure on launch, with great promises and an underwhelming delivery. No Man's Sky: the game that was cursed from the start actually turns out to be an amazing game!

I'm not joking! This game has seen a TON of FREE has been running ever since. Not smoothly, that is. Let's start with the cons. This game is really weird as far as optimizations goes. It originally has been developped for consoles and it shows: I had to go really deep into xml config files in order to make this game semi playable. And it still has a lot of visual bugs. The bright side of being a console title is that the controller support is excellent, although, why can't I map buttons like I want?

Other than that, and the in-game inventory system being an absolute pain, I can't see anything wrong! I really wish, tho that we could be two person or more aboard certain ships. A bit like Elite: Dangerous's multicrew.

Anyways, on to the pros. The visals are stunning, with bright and colourful planets, chonky-boi creatures and a great overall aesthetic. The game engine technology isn't particularly new (in fact it's quite outdated) but a great artistic direction certainly goes a long way in making a game look and feel nice. I'm glad to announce that the devs have taken a particular attention to the randomly generated planets and ecosystem, which were a bit "too much the same" in the old days. Now, they are quite varied, with different biomes, oceans and climates.

Ships controls are hella tight and very fun to use. I do not have access to a vr setup, but i'm told that it's a wonderful experience flying ships in vr. You can also interract with NPCs that do look and feel quite similar, but can trade you stuff, exchange their ship for your pile of junk and make you learn their language.

The in-game story is nice and quite engaging. It also forces you to unlock stuff, making you progress in the game.

All in all, while I do value good first impressions, there are certain times where expectations may be turned, and No Man's Sky is without no doubts one of those time. Would recommend, and i give it a SOLID 4/5!

This would be my favorite game if it wasn't too instable to play. Especially in a game that requires time intesive grinds to gather materials, I find it very upsetting to lose the last hour of gameplay because of a game freeze. The idea of having fixed save points could enhance the gameplay and make it more exciting and interesting BUT it only works with solid games, that allow me to actually reach those save points without locking up half my system. 

I play games for fun (shocking I know) and thinking the whole time that all I do might be for nothing just stresses me out. When I am done with work and I have 1-2h to spare, I would like to chill, relax, and make some progress and not get frustraded and disappointed over poor programming. 

Making it possible to save at any time in the game (excluding situations like immediate danger) would compensate for that problem to some degree. Not as a shortcut or to make the game easier - In fact, it doesn't make the game harder to save in specific locations - but to give the player the chance to minimize the damage and lost time caused by one of the very frequent crashes.

My computer is fine and well maintained. I don't experience crashes in games even if they have the reputation to crash often. This is currently the only game I can count on crashing at least once during a game session. Usually that's the end of the game session as well. 

I am not salty because the game crashes. I wouldn't even care that much. I just start it again. It is the attitude to place a save mechanism that doesn't reflect the code quality. I would prefer an honest save mechanism that takes into account that the game could freeze at any given time. 

While the gameplay is absolutely fun I can't get over the fact that I never left the game with a good feeling and as someone who values peoples time I can't recommend this game.

Reviews.111982:
I remember the fiasco of this game's launch. It was a mess of colossal proportions. But it's gotten better and better over time. I love it. I've had four characters across two versions of this game (Just a warning - get this version if you want to mod or edit saves. Game Pass version won't allow editing of the game files). This is part of the trifecta of good space games, and I love how it has a different feel than the other two. It's very quick to get in your ship and get going, and it's fun for casual play sessions as well as marathons. Some pros and cons, because you have to, right?

Pros:
-Beautiful, especially with the next-gen update and running on Ultra. Truly some amazing views.
-Procedural generation of planets and ships means you're unlikely to see the exact same thing twice
-Companions! You can finally tame that wildlife you see. It's not too useful, but a nice touch.
-Interesting story that is also entirely optional
-Truly a great community surrounds it
-Multiple galaxies of different types to explore, with millions of stars each. You'll never see it all.
-Creative mode for easy play, or you can mod for new content/QoL changes. You can even saveedit if you're a dirty cheater (but don't, though. It takes a lot of the fun out of it)
-Almost every resource can be harvested, but can also be bought in quantity once you have the green. DO THIS. You'll save hours harvesting materials by hand (especially di-hydrogen, which is very useful).
-Really good base building. I've seen some incredible designs (although all mine are boxes). You can have numerous bases, with teleporters linking them.
-You get to have a freighter, which is like a mobile base with tons of room to build, as well as hangar spots for all your ships. It also has a fleet of frigates you can use to do timed unattended missions for extra money/resources

Neutral
-A flight sim, this is not. Whether that's a pro or con is up to you. This is much more casual than Elite or SC. Personally, I play those games for the sim elements, so I'm okay getting in my ship and getting to orbit in ten seconds here.

Cons:
-You see soon enough that, while the universe is vast, there's not much point to it once you get far enough in.
-Finding exactly what you want can be a nightmare (thank god there's NMSCE)
-You can only have one freighter and six starships. Sounds like a lot, but you run out of slots pretty fast.
-Combat is a joke after the first few hours. Once you get S-class upgrades, there's not much to challenge you
-Those upgrades are expensive in rare materials, and don't transfer. So if you trade in your shuttle for that shiny new S-Class fighter, you're hunting all those upgrades again. Same applies for multi-tools (which is your do-everything weapon/tool)
-Money (as in credits) is SO easy to make. You'll be rolling in millions with minimal effort.
-Multiplayer is a bit wonky sometimes
-The game isn't terribly forthcoming with info. You'll be relying on reddit/wiki for a lot of info.

All in all, this is a very fun game, especially the first playthrough, and is a great game to put down and come back to after a few months. You'll get lost once again. Personally, I'd wait for a sale, or give it a whirl on Game Pass first. But if you like space exploration, you'll love this.

The game is nice and quite rich in content, however it lacks in quality. There is very little of survival elements, it's mostly exploration. The storyline is nothing special and the final explanation of all the anomalies is really lame, aka “you wake up and realise that your entire gameplay was just a dream”. All the times shown in game are actually real time, you can turn the game off and these activities will still progress - it's a shame that the game doesn't inform you about it...

[h1]Grinding, lots of it[/h1]

Very soon you find yourself doing the same things over and over again and it doesn't really get better as you progress through the game:
[list]
[*] There are three alien races with their own languages made of ~650 words each, which are identical in structure to English and you have to learn words one by one. And so you will be learning words such as “a”, “an” or “the”. After 250h in game I still only know about 1500 out of the 2000 words.
[*] On each planet there is plenty of minerals, animals and plants to scan (and scanning gives you money), but it is always as tedious as within the first minutes of the gameplay. No mass scanning, no scanning speed upgrade, nothing.
[*] You can trade, but this is usually in low quantities so you end up spending most time on the loading screens, just jumping between stations.
[/list]

[h1]Not a survival game[/h1]

Although you have to resupply your life support system with oxygen, recharge your shield to survive in hazardous environments and alien robots or animals can kill you, it's really difficult to achieve any of these. In fact, all the times I died was from my own grenades.

Your bases are indestructible, there are no turrets/traps to build, enemies stop chasing you as soon as you enter your base.

[h1]Nice things[/h1]

[list]
[*] Modifiable terrain (although only to certain depth) - you can mine, create land, flatten, restore to original.
[*] There is a lot of freedom when base building - you can make objects overlap or make them float in the air and they won't fall down.
[*] Navigation in space is quite easy thanks to the very convenient radar. You can easily see where nearby objects and enemy starships are and which direction you have to turn to see them in front of you.
[*] There is some sort of aim assist while shooting starships - it's nice, but I think it makes fights too easy.
[/list]

[h1]Critical issues and game breaking bugs[/h1]

Not many, but there are some and they can get really annoying when they happen. Especially, that you cannot save a game from the main menu. You have to build a special object used for saving the game - it's easy to carry it with you, but you generally cannot save the game in space.

[list]
[*] Community features don't work on Windows 7 unless you enable TLS - you will not see any errors in game. Unless you google search, you won't even know that you are missing on some special missions or easy money.
[*] Game sometimes crashes when building a base.
[*] I once got stuck in the conversation, forcing me to kill the game and load the previous save.
[*] I once warped to inside of my capital ship and got stuck within its structure...
[*] I once had my tool reverted to pre-upgraded version – it cost me a couple of difficult to find upgrade modules...
[/list]

[h1]A lot of minor bugs and quality of life issues[/h1]
[list]
[*] Game pauses on focus lost. It will even pause loading screens!
[*] Given how grindy the game is, conversations and missions handling takes far too much clicking and loading.
[*] You cannot assign mouse wheel up/down in the key mappings and certain mappings have collisions by default.
[*] Lots of bugs when base building - components don't snap to each other, a removed one cannot be placed back where it was etc.
[*] Sorting, filtering and searching issues - system are sorted by the time of first visit, stations are sorted by the time of last visit; no searching or filtering anywhere. Some lists have limits and drop the items from their bottom.
[*] Artificial limits to slow you down - you can place only 3 refiners next to each other, the next 3 have to be 20m away; automated mining drills have their output reduced if they deliver to a single storage depot etc.
[*] You cannot mass-craft items quickly - it's one key press per item.
[*] You can trade food for special currency, but only one at the time...
[*] Cannot remove basic weapon from tool/ship - if you have two better weapons installed, switching weapon will always rotate through that basic one (plus it wastes a module slot)
[*] From dozens of modules in your tools/vehicles/starships that need regular refuelling, only one can be automated.
[*] Personal Refiner in your exosuit keeps making refining sound and animation when it runs out of fuel, but the refining is actually stopped.
[*] You can upload your discoveries to get some special money and there is a button to upload them all at once, however the biggest amount of money is for discovering all animals on the planet and this can only be uploaded manually (which you first have to find by clicking through dozens of planets you have ever visited).
[*] Sometimes resources disappear from your refiners.
[*] Teleporting between stations takes ages (20+ seconds), even though the internals of all stations are identical.
[*] Planets that you scan from space are not added to discoveries list, you have to actually land on the planet.
[*] You cannot accurately compare tools/starships with what is available for purchase as the numbers shown include the upgrades you installed.
[*] Base Computer cannot be moved - it's a portable structure that you need to place on the ground to claim terrain for your base, but once you do so, you cannot move it.
[*] Foundations/columns cannot be placed in the air, making them useless.
[*] A full screen pop-up every time you visit a system, even if you visited it before, requiring you to hold a key for a few seconds to close it.
[*] Star systems have planets and moons, but they have no stars. In the galaxy map, there is one bright point, brighter than any stars: https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2420794048
[/list]

I've never written a review on Steam before until this game.  If you read my entire review, thank you for jumping into my mind and seeing why I am leaving a 10/10 on this game.  And to be honest, most of the games I mention and play usually sit at a 8 or 9 /10 with me.  So I guess, where to start... well that depends on what you are looking for.  This game to me fulfills every category I've always looked for in a game.  Plus the game offers multiplayer and has an extraordinary community.  If you like and wished for Minecraft, Fallout 4, and Red Dead Redemption style games to have a baby with its genre or subcategories, then you'll have no issue jumping into the game.  

MINECRAFT - When i say its like Minecraft, I mean it in a sense of being on your own and having to work/grind for material to build and survive.  Each planet is entirely different than the next, like how Minecraft changes when you travel to a different biome.  Mining is a huge reason I mention Minecraft as well because you can literally change the terrain around you and gather it's resources that will help you build, upgrade, and survive.

FALLOUT 4 - The only main reason I include the Fallout 4 title is because of the base building concept of the game and its companion system.  And no it does not include turrets or defensive systems but makes up with in my opinion a broader spectrum inside of the building categories that Fallout 4 allows you to do with bases.  Plus there isn't a green boundary line for your base.  As for a companion, each planet offers different look of it's native animals.  It is impossible to find the same looking animal in another planet and the great part is you can have up to 6 different animals as a companion incase you want multiple.  They're breedable as well if you find that special one.

RED DEAD REDEMPTION - The few reasons I include Red Dead is because the main fanbase drawn to Red Dead is the need for exploration and making your name branded as you please.  The exploration is phenomenal!  They'res thousands upon thousands of planets and hundreds upon hundreds of galaxies to explore and each one offers something different from the last whether it is the color of the grass to the variation of trees and plants scattered across each planet.  And each planet takes some VERY serious dedication to explore it's entirety due to their vast and endless seeming size.  Now when I say branding your name, you are essential a cowboy with a hip shooter having a spaceship as your horse.  Each galaxy you enter has a dominant lifeform (Fraction of species essentially) that inhabits it, and you can choose who you want on your good side and your bad side.  If you want to be an outlaw and rob a cargo ship, go ahead.  If you want to be a bounty hunter and make some money, the world is yours.  And to top it off, this game is cross-platform and online, I play the game on my PC with some buddies on Playstation.

There is no right or wrong way to play this game, it is truly at your will.  I can say the last time I felt passionate about a game like this was when Oblivion the elder scrolls came out on PS3.  I fascinate with games that give me my own free will to explore with no borders, live by my own set of rules, and pioneer my own path.  If this fascinates you too then I would highly suggest this game as your next reason to spend that stimulus check on this truly unique game.  God bless America!

I really enjoyed my time playing NMS. The game looks good in a cartoony sort of way and, for a while at least, the variety in the planets is really nice. After a while the planets do start to get a bit samey and there really isn't much benefit in exploring other than for the odd photo opportunity or the possibility of finding a wrecked ship.
The main story quest is ok, but is nothing to write home about. Once you get that out of the way and unlock the stargate portals etc, the game properly opens up.
Hats off to Hello Games who have churned out a lot of new features for this game, and do so at no extra cost to the consumer.
In that respect they put companies like Frontier and Elite Dangerous to shame.
Where I have issue with NMS is the endgame...all these extra things that have been added to the game are good, but pretty shallow. The in game vehicles are all pretty pointless other than providing a bit of extra storage space. If you want to get somewhere you will inevitably use your spaceship once it is properly kitted out. 
On the topic of the spaceships, I find that they are all pretty much the same. You can upgrade a fighter to hold the same amount of cargo as a trader, the only choice seems to be aesthetic when it comes down to it.
The space based combat is really basic, and the enemy AI is pretty poor and predictable. So having a freighter instead of a fighter seems to make no difference. There are arbitrary differences in jump range etc, but even that doesn't have much of an impact on the game as you can portal everywhere and your ship magically goes with you. The living ships are great, but the story arc to get one is terrible.
The giant freighters that you get are really cool and make great mobile bases. You can even have a fleet of ships to send away on missions which is cool, but is pretty superfluous.
There are missions to explore derelict freighters, but these quickly become repetitive.
Base building is fun. I made a few industrial bases to generate cash and I visited a few amazing looking bases that were created by other players. Other than the industrial/creative aspect of base building, there isn't really much more to it...there are no planet based enemies that will try to raid it or destroy it, and you don't need it to survive.
All in all, 200+ hours for a game that cost me £15 is money well spent. However, I honestly can't see myself going back to the game anytime soon...it would take a significant content upgrade (perhaps paid for?) to draw me back in.

I waited until 2020 to get and try this game- and I am glad I did so, as it allowed me to experience the game free from the distortion of expectation that so many of us had at the time of release.

The world fell in love with No Man's Sky when it was still just an embryo of ideas, visions, and potential.
The world turned to hating No Man's Sky when the reality of a complex situation showed its ugly head and people's expectations- unreasonable or not- were not met.

The folks at Hello Games have big dreams as well as the courage to pursue them.
They took a big risk and expended great deal of time, energy, and love into this game, and even though the launch didn't live up to the hype- and the hate they received was overwhelming, they continue to work on and update the game at no cost to their customers.  
Their simulated universe is becoming more fleshed out as time goes on. Big updates have brought new features and content to the game- many have room to be further improved upon, promising a richer, deeper, more captivating experience down the line.

I suggest you try the game, even if you have before, and allow yourself to experience it for what it is instead of a conglomeration of what everyone wanted it to be. It's given me a great deal of new experiences and pleasure during one of the crappiest years in recent history.

2021 No Man's Sky is a fantastic game, and it's only been getting better over time. It's not perfect, it never was, probably won't ever be. But it's certainly worth your time. As of right now, this game has:

Colorful, random, and wacky planets to explore
A fairly long and rewarding main story quest
Side quests/missions
Base building, farming, and cooking
Space ships with thousands of variations
Fleet vehicles that can be used for a mobile base or sent on quests for gathering resources 
Ground vehicles
Research trees for guns, resource scanners, vehicles, and ships
Upgrades for customizing and improving your ships, tools, vehicles, etc.
Pets that can be tamed and bred
Customizable character appearance
Space pirates (you can also be a pirate and attack faction ships for resources)
Great music
You can name planets, creatures, etc. while planets discovered by you are marked as such for other players to see

There are still plenty of things to be improved. Set your expectations accordingly:

Ground/space combat is very simple; the AI is pretty poor
Base building can be fairly limited without utilizing bugs to expand piece placement/options
Cooking has limited uses outside of turning in dishes to sell despite a huge list of items
The difficulty of exploring is fairly limited in normal difficulty and quickly scales off as you upgrade your suit
The game can be pretty ambiguous about how to advance your character (besides the main story)

Overall, the game is quite enjoyable and is only getting better. The universe is yours to explore, traveler.

No Man's Sky is a wacky, fun and exciting space exploration game I'd  recommend to anyone who is on the fence or new to the genre. The mechanics are simple yet well designed and in depth. It's quick to pick up but offers hours of entertainment.

Pros:
- Visually beautiful
- Generally smooth gameplay
- Hours of content
- A dedicated Dev team constantly improving the game
- A great central player hub full of side content to explore

Cons:
- Flying can be a little wonky at times
- Planets can get a little bland at times (Constantly improving though)
- There could be more side varied missions
- The beginning is very slow, you have to dedicate time to explore and build yourself up (Only a con if you're a speed player)

For me personally, the pros vastly outweigh the cons. No Man's Sky has made an excellent recovery thanks to an amazing dev team, seriously, if you guys read this, you're awesome for sticking with this ambitious game.

I got this game around December 2020 on PC and I have been play everyday since. 
This is what the game gets right!
Exploration
        You find new planets, animals, plants, new spaceships because the game procedurally generates all of this when you go to a galaxy map, pick a star to explore, and travel there. You can always find new stuff in this game because this game is designed to mimic an infinite universe. 
Spaceships
        There's fighter ships, huge storage ships, fast exploring ships, and even alien lifeforms that turn into living ships! You find all these ships by exploring!
base building
         You can build farms, mines, portal stations, and even paradise mansions! You need to find resources and blueprints by exploring!
animal companions
        Every animal you find will be cataloged and named like a space traveling zoologist! When you find an animal you like you can give it a pet treat, make a new friend, and take them with you on your adventures. You and your companion help each on exploring!
multiplayer experience 
        You summon a traveling space station. Inside it you find other players and travelers like you. You find every kind of spaceship from other players, you see new customized appearances, new companions that everyone brought from the universe, and finally you do missions with other people that require your group to complete missions of exploration!

Every feature in the game is all in the pursuit of exploring infinite universes! If you don't like exploring, space travel, or infinite possibilities then this is not the game for you. 

This is what is wrong with the game.
visual glitches still (apparently since 2016)
         It still  has visual glitches like animals walking throw rocks. Summoning a huge spaceship that strangely changes a different color. You load a game save and your character's texture has not fully loaded in. These are described as technical issues with the game. These types of glitches appear roughly 15% of the time I play everyday.
Infinite universe but limited design
          When you explore several galaxies and universes, you can not find a single city with a big population of aliens to explore. The game is not designed for that feature yet! You upgrade technology to the cutting edge until there is nothing else to upgrade and you have done everything the game has to offer. Now you are left in the end game fly from star to star, system to system, planet to planet because that is the only feature in the game that has something for you to do. I suppose the only limit is the developers of hello games imaginations, their time management, their programming, and their dedication to the themes of this wonderful space genre. 

Hello games is doing a wonderful job with this game. I feel this way about this game because right now this game is great! 
If they are dedicated to the players of this game now, then I am dedicated to them and their success. that's it!

Reviews.112524:
Ah, No Man's Sky! The great success-story! Despite launching with hardly any of the promised features, successive updates - all free, mind! - have added just about everything that was originally claimed to be there, and then some! Indeed, they're STILL adding new stuff! So why the thumbs-down? 

BECAUSE THEY KEEP ADDING STUFF! This game is basically in a permanent Beta-state - or perhaps 'Early Access' is a better term, considering the platform. And as a result, it is pouring bugs OUT OF EVERY ORIFICE. Every new patch, every new content-expansion, every new addition, introduces new bugs, because of course it does... and then only the most egregious of crashes, the most serious of showstoppers, and the most gnarly gamebreakers get fixed, 'cuz hey, they're already busy on the NEXT big content-update!

Thus, all the LITTLE bugs are left unfixed, for years and years, and just keep mounting up, and up, and up, until no aspect of the game can be said to actually WORK properly. I mean, a game of this type, it's very much up to you to decide what you want it to be ABOUT... there's no true 'win-state', after all, so you get to pick for yourself what you want to focus on! Maybe you want to build awesome bases on scenic alien planets? Maybe you want to try and cook every food-recipe in the game? Or collect all the cosmetics, or all the player titles? Or perhaps you just want to have fun running some missions with a friend or two in multiplayer?

Well, TOUGH LUCK, 'cuz no matter WHAT you decide to focus on, it isn't working - your progress will be endlessly stymied by bugs, bugs, bugs, glitches, crashes, bugs, glitches, and bugs. Wanna make an awesome base? Sure, go right on ahead, just remember not to leave the refinery unattended while you're cooking up materials, otherwise they output AND the fuel will spontaneously disappear. And those blueprints you just bought? Yeah, they don't actually exist - you can't make them. Those other ones? They DO exist, but they don't click together properly,  so they'll clip into each other in a rather ugly fashion. Oh, and did you dig out some land to make a basement, or level a hill to make room for a landing-pad? Well, next time you return, all that will be undone, so now your landing-pad is under a hill and your basement is full of dirt. Fun times!

Focusing on collecting stuff instead? Well, I hope it isn't food-recipes, 'cuz some of them just flat-out don't work, and others are impossible since certain ingredients just don't spawn where they're supposed to. Titles? Some of them just don't actually award when they should. Cosmetics? You'll need Quicksilver for those, awarded by Nexus Missions - pick 'em carefully, 'cuz some of them are bugged and impossible to complete, while others have to be approached very delicately due to the messed-up way the game records your progress - move too quickly, and your actions won't be recorded, making the mission incompletable!

Multiplayer fun? Hah! Good luck! Just being IN multiplayer makes everything way more likely to spontaneously break, and you'll probably soon wind up in parallel realities - unable to see or interact with each other despite being in the same spot, unable to see each other's bases or ships, unable to join missions together. Of course, the Nexus Missions are what you're SUPPOSED to be doing together, assuming you can find your way into the same dimension long enough to join up - see above warning!

For a while, you may be able to push through, ignore the bugs, focus on the good, but they just keep mounting, and you'll notice more and more of them until you just can't take it anymore. So just... don't. Maybe someday, when they finally stop adding more crap to it, and take the time to actually FIX the stuff they've ALREADY GOT - when they get the game as a whole to a complete, stable, and halfway polished state - THEN AND ONLY THEN will it be worth buying.

As for me, I've got 200 hours in there, and I regret approximately 150 of them. I guess 50 hours of fun isn't a bad payout, but that's a really poor ratio overall...

If you're a fan of space games then definitely check this one out. It's unique enough to grab on a discount.
After almost finishing the game (would finish it today but I got bugged on the last ATLAS mission) I decided to think about my experience and leave a review.
At the start of the game it tickles the right feelings - an unknown world that you're free to explore. Great!
Unfortunately the game tries very hard to artificially slow you down. Meaningless dialog, unskipable animations, odd choice for the ATLAS sprint progress [spoiler]visit 10 ATLAS interfaces to get 10 blueprints for something that might aswell have been a single blueprint[/spoiler], many idle mechanics (you have to wait real hours/days for fleet missions and plant growth) many quests that depend on you explicitly warping your ship instead of teleporting... unfortunately I had to wiki on many occasions just to figure out that I'm not getting mission updates because I'm sitting on my butt waiting just for that.
The game quickly becomes an unrewarding grind where you mainly teleport around and barely even need to use your ship (except for the main questline which forces you to travel through many systems - of course as soon as you jump you just go back to the map and jump again, repetition and a waste of time). The infinite universe becomes very tiny once you see the repeating elements.
It's a unique experience in the sense that you probably won't have an opportunity to play a game that's [i]misdesigned[/i] like this. The ambition was there, the art is great, sound design is ok, not a fan of the music style, the storyline was interesting for the first few hours and then I realised it's not really worth the attention... Unfortunately the game does not deliver on it's promises. Anyway it's an interesting case to study [i]what went wrong[/i]. If you're not feeling like experimenting and potentially being disappointed then look at some other games.
All that being said - I think the developers are doing a good job with the updates. Some of the new features were what convinced me to try and check the game out after the bad kickoff. I'm sure they're pouring their hearts into this project, I'm hoping their next game is a success that they deserve.

Reviews.112530:
I've played this game for about 300 hours on Normal. Didn't read any how to's or watch any videos to learn the game in the beginning, wanted to do that myself. Its definitely grabs you from the start.  

Everything is great looking, some planets are just amazing looking. Trying to go from space hobo to intergalactic industrialist is fun. Figuring out how to make credits in the beginning was challenging since I didn't yet know the items and tricks that make credit earning trivial.

Looking for cool ships...and being able to afford them was fun. I now have a tie fighter look-a-like, a slave I (boba fetts ship) look-a-like, a tricked out hauler ( although I'm trying to find one that resembles the Razor Crest (mandalorian) ) and a exotic...to top it off I have a freighter that looks like a star destroyer....I'm a bit of a star wars fan if ya didnt notice.

Base building is a bit tricky but I've managed to make some pretty cool looking cribs. Had to go to the steam forums to learn about glitches and tricks to make things work sometimes which isn't ideal.

Ok so all the stuff above makes for a pretty cool game...but heres the thing....there are bugs...lots of them. Some break your saved game (rare from what I've seen) and some are slow dripping water torture type bugs that eat away at you. 

One example that drives me batty is the tab inventory...you will have inventory pages for your suit, ship, gun/multitool, etc....there is no way to keybind specific inventories...only tab opens inventories then there are pages for each one, and the game, it seems, likes to open every inventory accept the one you use most (exosuit).

So you must manually switch to exosuit after you hit tab....not game breaking, but when you go into inventory a few hundred times with this bug bring up the wrong one it can be....triggering. Theres community found tricks that fix it for a little bit but it always breaks again and from what I've read this little bug has been around for a long time without a fix so dont count on fixes.

Then there are the intentional annoyances that hello games put in for whatever reason, like not being allowed to put more than a few refiners in the same area of a base, the monotonous way refiners in general work is not ideal for mass refining of materials either.  The way storage is designed makes inventory management a mini game...or chore in itself...but fear not if you want to make a industrial base with rows of shiny refiners there are glitches to make it work, and addons can make the game's not so great time sinks more tolerable....even though I don't think we should need to do that for a $60 game. 

If you can overlook the bugs and learn about the addons then I think this is a game you would enjoy, heck I wrote the good and bad above and still have the desire to play after 300 hours....but not for $60. Wait for a sale.

Reviews.112545:
[quote]Like this review? Find more reviews on my curator group, [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/37886957-Bog-Boy/?appid=449960]Bog Boy[/url]!

I made a new curator group for long-form reviews, [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/40044190-Jewel-Case-Reviews/]Jewel Case Reviews![/url]
[/quote]
[h1]📑 Overview[/h1]
[i][b]This review contains no spoilers.[/b][/i]

No Man's Sky is a first-person or third-person (Camera type is hot-swappable) open-world survivalcraft game set in a sci-fi setting. The player takes control of an unnamed "anomaly" who wakes up on a hostile planet with no recollection of their origins. 

No Man's Sky has received a ton of controversy back when it was first released in 2016 due to unmet promises made during development. However, the game's developers, Hello Games, have proven to be extremely capable of revitalizing what seemed like a lost cause. 

[table]
[tr]
[th]🟢 Pros[/th]
[th]🟠 Cons[/th]
[/tr]
[tr]
[th]
- Game looks great, even at minimum settings.
- Mining resources is satisfying and easy. 
- The randomly-generated landscapes and wildlife are almost always unique and bring a sense of wonder to the world.
- Flying starships feels very good.
[/th]
[th]
- While much better than when it released, the game is still filled with bugs of varying levels of impact. 
- Multiplayer is subpar.
[/th]
[/tr]
[/table]

[table]
[tr][th]💾 Hardware[/th][/tr]
[tr][th]CPU: AMD Ryzen 5 3600
GPU: NVIDIA GTX 1060 3GB
RAM: 16 GB
OS: Windows 10
Display: 1080p 60hz
[/th][/tr][/table]

[h1]📖 Story[/h1]
The player awakens on a hostile planet and must quickly get their bearings before they are killed by the cold, heat, or radiation of the world they spawn in. After installing various technologies to help them traverse the alien landscape, the player is made aware of a distress signal, which strangely just repeats the same code: [16,16,16]. The player seems to be following the trail of a person who came long before them and soon takes to the stars in search of the origin of the signal. 

The story in No Man's Sky is clearly there to guide along the tutorial and propel player exploration, and it works fine in doing that. The story teaches the player important mechanics such as resource mining, material refinement, crafting, starship flight, and hyperwarping in a fairly intuitive and non-intrusive way. 

No Man's Sky is a sandbox game where you are supposed to make your own goals. The basic story gives the player an idea of what those goals can be, and keeps the game open ended enough that the player can ignore the story and just get right into the experience.

[h1]🎮 Gameplay[/h1]
Gameplay in No Man's Sky is varied and wide-rangedl, but what you will be doing most of the time is flying in a starship between planets and other locations. I have to say that it's impressive how fun it is to control the starships. A lot of the starship's maneuvers feel really awesome to carry out. I haven't personally touched much of space combat, but from what I have experienced, it feels super cool to dodge asteroids and doing quick turnarounds to attack the enemy with laser cannons or missiles. It's just plain fun.

Another common thing you will be doing is exploring planets on foot. The movement speed of the player feels perfect, and there are other movement options to help the player to traverse the alien worlds. While exploring, the player will often find minerals or ore deposits that they will want to collect. This is where the multitool comes in -- the multitool works like a mining laser, terrain manipulator, or even a laser gun. Resource collection with the mining laser is satisfying and quick, and can be upgraded to be even quicker and reap more rewards. 

Exploration is the big draw to this game, and the various ways you can explore keeps the game fresh. Part of the reason why exploration feels really good is because you can name the things you can find. Most explorable things are randomly generated, which means that each planet is unique, and there will always be more stuff to find.

Combat appears pretty rarely unless the player decides to attack a creature without provocation. If you avoid sentinel-filled planets, you're generally gonna be pretty safe and not die often as long as you pay attention to your hazard protection. I'm fine with this, as ground combat outside of an exocraft is pretty mediocre. It's just hold left click on the enemy and don't get hit. 

There is just too much to talk about in regards to gameplay to fit in this review, but just keep in mind that there's almost always something to do. Whether you like trading, exploring, combat, or base building, there will always be some sort of task for you to pick up. However, No Man's Sky is all about creating your own goals. If you want a game that gives you a clear objective, this game is simply not for you. 

However, there is one facet of gameplay I have not gone over, and that is multiplayer. The concept behind No Man's Sky's multiplayer is that you can run into other players while exploring the universe. While that sounds cool, the universe in No Man's Sky is theoretically infinite. You could be online for thousands of hours, but there's almost zero chance you're going to naturally run into another player. You are also supposedly able to see what other people have named things that they have discovered, but I have had issues getting that to work properly, even when directly playing with some of my friends. On that note, directly joining a friend is basically just teleporting you to them in their session. There is no co-op element to the multiplayer. If that's not what you need, then the multiplayer will suit you: but I expected some semblance of co-op mechanics (like quest synchronization or a refined trading menu) and was disappointed. 

[h1]🕵 Audiovisuals and Performance [/h1]
Graphically, No Man's Sky is picturesque, despite being almost all randomly generated. There is a powerful photo mode, and at almost any time during the game you could open the photo mode and take a really nice picture with minimal effort. I played this game at the lowest settings, and the game still managed to put me in awe at some of its scenery. The animations for alien races are incredibly emotive, helping to make these fantastical alien species seem more real. 

The game performs okay but leaves a lot to be desired. While the overall game looks visually pleasing, the graphics themselves are not great if you look at them for too long. I feel that No Man's Sky is probably not the most well optimized and could look a whole lot nicer on lower end builds if some extra effort was put into optimizing it. 

The game is buggy sometimes, as well. The worst I have had is a broken main quest, where I had to use a save editor to move the quest forward. I was willing to do this, but most players will not be. Hello Games have been doing an amazing job at cleaning up this game, but the game is still not perfect in regards to bugs. However, the game is constantly being updated and these issues may be lessened in the future.

[h1]📗 Closing Opinions[/h1]
[b]FINAL VERDICT: GOOD[/b]
★★★★☆
No Man's Sky has made one heck of a comeback compared to how it was at launch and has plenty of content to play with as long as you are willing to make your own goals. The scenery is majestic, and the world feels real, with each planet managing to have its own personality in the literally infinite universe. However, the game is far from perfect. It's still filled with bugs, ranging from mild inconveniences that could probably be amusing, to game-breaking. The multiplayer also leaves a bit to be desired. Overall, the pros outweigh the cons in most respects, and No Man's Sky is a really fun experience that I could see people putting hundreds, if not thousands of hours into.

Its been a long time since I've played a game because it is genuinely enjoyable and not just because I am depressed and have nothing better to do. This game constantly throws both pleasant and nerve-racking surprises at the player.  The creative way in which Hello Games has cleverly approached common open-world multiplayer issues is something to be admired by other developers.  One thing they could definitely improve however would be making multiplayer feel more meaningful.  Currently i am trying to play with my friends and it feels like we are in the same place always doing different things. if the game had more team work related game-play and allowed more than 4 players in a group, i doubt we would be able to stop playing.

Things I could recommend:

- make sentinals appear in larger groups more consistently in order to make blowing up hundreds of ships for free loot more of a challenge (perhaps even hard enough that having a few friends would make it possible)

- perhaps add a couple more factions and languages to the game that suddenly start wars with the already existing factions that the player can choose sides in and fight other players for sections of the galaxy or star systems (obviously this is a stretch, but it would make the end game much more meaningful)

- optimise freighters better for use by multiple players (or else what is the point of freighters aside from a mini side tycoon)

overall however, This game has grown so much since i first played in 2016. I am having an amazing time with it and i am excited to see what else Hello Games decides to do next.

So much to do in this game! I still don't know what the hell is going on, but I've been having a blast figuring it out!

UPDATE 50hrs
OMG I just figured out how to board the capital ships I've been robbing!!! After robbing this fleet, I boarded and then offered to buy the fleet (2 ships), and then I was challenged by competing merchants (Guess I wandered into their trade route), destroyed them, and I just had to put in here how amazing this is!!! UPDATE 78 HRS
I played 70 hours before deciding to focus a little on the story, and I'm now seeing what a great job they did writing it! They seem to have gotten an actual Sci-fi writer on this game. The writing is absolutely amazing. I'm amazed at how long and how far I was able to get without really even doing the storyline, and how much there is to do as well. Playing this 2000s style (without looking at guides or videos, just figuring this game out myself) and must say, it reminds me of how awesome it was playing Morrowind for the first time on Xbox before internet was an everyday thing. Very rewarding!

My favorite part is teleporting my space armada directly into orbit above my planet and watching from the ground at how amazing and large it looks. Breathtaking! The dogfights in space are pretty fun as well! It would be amazing if they added the ability to bombard locations by calling artillery strikes from space while standing on the ground, as well as calling in fighter support from the ground. Also, it would be very cool if they would let you have the option of joining your fleets on expeditions. The way they tell the events at the end of them make these seem super exciting!

This game quickly loses its luster after you've been to a few systems and planets. They all generally follow environmental themes (fire planet, toxic planet, oceanic planet, dust planet, barren planet, tropical planet). You won't land on a planet full of civilization, just space stations with carbon copy NPCs that all say the same thing. A game of this promised magnitude should've been in development for 12-15 years, crap launch, but their dedication to this IP is admirable. 

The freighter system lacks any semblance of feeling like a captain/commander of a star fleet. You can send the ships you have out on missions, they warp out, some hours pass by, they warp in and report and give you loot. You can't assist on the missions or tag along on one of the ships that are going. You can't pilot the freighter if you wanted and many rooms built on mine were glitched out. 

The quests are woefully buggy still. Some NPCs I got for my home base remained stuck in a quest loop. The exploration diminishes by your 6th planet or 3rd galactic jump. The animals are procedural mutants and unbelievable, some are uniquely put together, but for me, it was rare. You can kill animals, and domesticate them for a short while, but after a while they'll reset and roam around. Wish I could take one of the small cute pets with me to other systems as a travel buddy, you sadly cannot. 

Character customization is a bit deep but not too much. There is no ship customization, I can deal with most cockpits on ships resembling each other, but it really breaks immersion when you see an EXACT copy of your ship land right next you in a space station. Seriously, it sucks that you can't color customize your personal craft (maybe you can, I don't know how too) you can however customize the color of your freighter, that's ok. 

This game is as wide as our own unexplored universe, but reveals its true self as part of the story, NMSs universe is only a dying simulation going through countless iterations until the final master system eventually corrupts and destroys itself. So I can completely forgive the constant imbalance and issues, it's a bit ingenious. I played this game altered and some of the literary concepts spoke to me philosophically, but after realizing the limitations of NMSs simulated universe, I didn't care anymore about the pursuit to the center to find any continued answer. 

I wish we were able to go back into deteriorated iterations to see what past Travellers built or did. But alas, we are left to comb through many decaying copies of the same universe to find help for an AI we really don't care about. What I think the developers should've done was take less of a grandiose approach of universal volume and limit the systems we could explore. Build a full pre-story galaxy that truly sets us up for our travels with an immersive story, species and background where we learn, that for some reason many explored parts of the universe is barren or are becoming barren THEN let us loose to save/civilize that universe ONLY to find out we're in some machine. Then slowly open up the universe (through seasonal releases) as you fine tune the algorithm for the procedurally generated galaxy, planets and life systems. 

I would LOVE to recommend this game because it holds up the illusion of VASTNESS real well early on, but man does that illusion fade away quick. Its like I found myself kicked back into a younger 7 year old version of myself in an empty room with 10 space toys and told to play for 7 hours, excited at what you're given at first but then you feel isolation after the first 2 hours. The last thing I want to do is feel isolation when I'm exploring the universe, but the awkward NPCs, animals, planets and random interactions ALL made me feel isolated and alone. 

Purchase this on a nice sale or on a free weekend. Not a terrible buy, but not a good one. Game on my friends!

I also know the game is not entirely focused on space ships like Elite is, but it is a fundamental part of the game, and more ship gameplay would have been much more appreciated than the ability to have a space dog.

Verdict - Buy this game if it is on sale, it can be alot of fun. However I can still only recommend paying full price if space/sci-fi Minecraft is just your thing.

No Man's Sky is the perfection of what I wanted so many other Sci-Fi games to be.

The planet exploration is what I wanted from Mass Effect; the space combat and trading are what I wanted from Elite Dangerous and EVE Online; the character development and RPG mechanics are what I wanted from Fallout; the visuals are what I wanted from Destiny; the resource-gathering and building are what I wanted from Starbound.

No Man's Sky is not any of the aforementioned games, and I don't think it "replaces" them, but it does do a great job of scratching certain itches that those games left me with.

I have been playing in permadeath mode (read: replaying the beginning a lot), so there is much more to No Man's Sky that I haven't seen yet, including multiplayer. However, I feel like I'm seeing the tip of the iceberg in terms of depth and complexity, so I can only imagine it will get better from here.

Very fun exploration/construction game with a lot going on. There are several ways to progress in the game, several ways to make money, several ways to earn blueprints... all kinds of different ships, freighters, pets, tools, and millions of planets such that it's weird when someone else has discovered a place you go. I'm really impressed with this game.

Everything is procedurally generated, so a lot of the worlds and monsters are pretty similar. 
There are still opportunities for improvement, though. The planets could stand to have a few different biomes, at least at the poles and around the equator. I've seen a little variation on one side of a planet freom the other in some planet types, but it's mostly either "land" or "water". That said, there are some absolutely insane world types out there, and some seriously weird animals. Unfortunately many of the coolest critters I've seen can't be tamed, hopefully more targets will be added.

Thus far I haven't seen much of interest in the water despite the inclusion of a submarine. We'll see if that changes.

Do some research before you start, there are a lot of things to be aware of... good luck; have fun!

Reviews.112924:
It is a love - hate relationship, really.

Even though you can explore countless sun systems in different galaxies the game also has a good story that catches your interest. The mechanics are well adjusted, for my taste, though flying for the first time might need some getting used to. The worlds you can explore can look like everything, from stunningly beautiful to bizzare to completely artificial and weird. I am amazed every time I look up to the sky and see those beautiful other planets in the system. The weather changes on the planets (cold, heat, poison, radiation, etc.) and the variating atmosphere make the survival a challenge sometimes.
The plants and creatures on planets look mostly surprising I'd say and are very alike on every planet, though not always quite the same.

If you take your time following the Storyline, you should be finished with the main story at about 40-50 hours of gameplay.
You can play with up to four other people in a group, you can see every other player in the game though if multiplayer is enabled and if they are near you/ in the area around you.

Having found a neat planet you like, you can build a base, actually build multiple bases on one or more planets. The base building itself can be hard to coordinate though it has improved a lot over the years and the devs are further working on improving the game in every matter. 

Besides the Story and Planets there are also different anomalies that occur in space, abandoned buildings to explore, ships, freighters, etc.

now, what I hate about the game is, it doesnt save your personal progress, you need to save it yourself either manually through building a saving spot or leaving your ship also saves your game. The world around you though is saved automatically so if you get some copper off the planet for example and then your game crashes, which doesn't happen rarely to me at least (once or twice every 10 hours of playing especially after a new major update) and load your file, you no longer have the copper but the world does not contain that ore anymore as well. So that kinda sucks :/ Dying in general sucks. I died many ways in that game which were not my fault like spawning and immediately falling through the ground and dying of fall damage. Or spawning while your ship is flying around in the air without you is annoying. Or you build a base and the terrain you just edited and removed simply respawns to say "haha now you can do it all over again" in your face.

But to be honest the good side of the games makes it all worth. At least for me :3 
If you like open world exploration with (kinda optional) good storyline you should definetly try it. I'd wait til it's on steam sale though, the usual price is a bit high imo. 

Take your time with this gem and enjoy it ^^

Honestly I was skeptical when I purchased this, even long after the catastrophic market failure of its release. The game I believe is in a pretty good spot now, its got working multiplayer, missions for you and your friends to attempt, cool end game features like a living ship and derelict ships, base building and rovers of all sorts to explore the planets you find, shops and a steady progression system. As im writing this I have 110 hours and i still havent quite accomplished everything.

That being said there are a few things you might notice to make your experience not very fun. Derelict ships I feel are my biggest complaint. They're decently new but there only seems to be 2-3 scenarios of ship. You board a ship the first time and are careful and slow but after ship 3-4 you start to run through because they are predictable. 
The progression system is quite steady but GOOD GOD is it SLOOOOW. The tutorial took me near 3hours to complete, and my brother almost stopped playing due to it. Getting to THE ANOMALY is where I think the game truly opens up because it gives you access to the actual progression system instead of limiting you to 5-6 research objects. Until you get there, you feel very alone, broke, and useless, which may be exactly what they wanted, but I feel it could be sped up a bit by skipping the interplanetary stations until AFTER the anomaly visit. 

Other than that, there may be a few bugs or glitches here and there, but most every game offers wonderful things like that. Overall I would say the game is now worth it's full price and it keeps getting FREE updates, such as the new companions update which allows you to tame all those randomly generated creatures you stumble across.

And if none of this floats you boat, it has VR capabilities and it is quite fun, although a bit disorienting when in the ship.

[h1]Made me feel something for a game I have not felt in years[/h1]

[b]Before I make this review, let me give you some background information about the type of person I am.[/b]

 I am in my later 20s, I've been a gamer since daipers, I understand gaming and geek culture on a intuitive level, and as such, I am no casual at games in general. But as of the last 5-6 years I have been getting driven away from video games. Industry practices such as micro transactions, unfinished/mediocre products demanding full price, loot boxes and games being brain drained to accomodate more....ahem....a more "casual" crowd....if your anything like me, you know immediately all the problems I am outlining and perhaps a few more I have not mentioned, but the point is, all of this, combined with my own increased responsiblity as a adult, have made me very disillusioned with a passion that was once central to my identity.

[b]Games just werent doing it for me anymore[/b]

Aside from TW, it was either, no game was fun to me anymore, or I was too disgusted with the greedy practices that had become common place. For a long while I begin to think if this was the direction games were going, then despite my entire life having been around this hobby, I was no longer going to be a gamer. I began to focus on real life much more and felt myself becoming like a typical boomer, simply scoffing at people who waste their lives playing these mediocre trash heaps that dare call themselves games today. I was done with games.

[b]But then I saw a video from the youtuber, Internet Historian...[/b]

A incredibly detailed essay of a small game developer, struggling to push out a ambitious game, and failing to meet the deadline. Being crucified for their failure. Bouncing back, staying strong, fixing their mistakes, turning it all around, and refusing to charge extra for it......it inspired me. So much so that I went and bought No Man's Sky right away. And at half price too !

[b]The game immediately impressed me[/b]

Not only did I like this game.....but it made me feel the heart throb of the type I have not felt since.....well...years. It made me feel again, what playing a good game is like. I do not have much time in my life but by god I spent as much of that time as I could diving into this well crafted masterpeice of a space exploration simulator. Traveling through warp space and arriving to the surface of a new planet, that feeling of mystique and wonder that it gives you, not knowing what you should expect, will you be eaten alive by carnivorous creatures, or greeted by beautiful and friendly lifeforms.

I cannot stress enough how jaded I am with video games. But this is a game where you buy it once, and are not charged for any extra content, and you get all updates for free. AND it is a good freaking game to boot. Trust me, if it can meet my standards and restore a jaded gamer into playing 22 hours in just a week, you might wanna give this one a try. In a landscape full of greedy devs who want every nickel, and for horrible products, No Man's Sky is a shining beacon, radiating it's light, obliterating the lies and deception of every other industry participant that had been fed to us over these years. If Hello Games can make this, then why are so many games these days so bad? There is no excuse.

So definitely try the game if you never have, it is fun for a bit, especially if you're more interested in base building and exploration than anything else I'd say it's a great game for you, but if you're into PvE combat/content then you'll enjoy the game for a bit but eventually you'll probably get bored of doing essentially the same tasks over and over again with no real goal to achieve and the nagging feeling that you want more.

I honestly can't recommend this game. I mean at this rate I'm wasting roughly 200 hours a month playing it. That's 200 hours a month I could be ..... mowing the lawn, washing the car, cleaning out the garage......

It really hits a lot of the things I like to do. A virtually unlimited universe to explore and build bases and collect materials to craft things and such. I have a freighter with 30 frigates and try to keep constant missions going to see what cool items I get especially upgrades for my fleet. I do a lot of hunting for distress beacons to collect crashed starships to salvage.

I've seen a couple reviews that were rather negative about how hard the survival part was at first. I personally didn't find it hard at all. But then I have a few hundred hours into ARK Survival Evolved..... In that game I spawned in an "Easy" area and quickly discovered you could punch trees like in Minecraft to get wood and thatch so I used that and some stones I picked up from the beach and crafted a lovely stone pickaxe and got to like level 2. Unfortunately before I could use the pickaxe a level 27 carnataur ran up and ate me. When I respawned I quickly saw a backpack with a streamer going into the sky marking the location of my precious pickaxe and also saw the carnataur patrolling around it to keep me from retrieving it. Unfortunately it saw me too. Since I was running anyhow I figured I'd make a dash for the backpack to get the pickaxe. When I respawned I found I could crawl so thought I could possibly sneak up and determine which of the two backpacks contained the pickaxe but the carnataur had very sharp eyes. When I respawned I found I had spawned right between the legs of the carnataur. Now if you or I had a tasty snack suddenly spawn between our legs we would most likely pause a moment to ponder how that happened. The carnataur didn't. When I respawned I chose a DIFFERENT part of the map but still EASY and proceeded to punch a tree to make another pickaxe BUT a pack of 3 raptors had other ideas and the level 12 was credited with the kill. After a couple times of that I decided to try the original area I had spawned and found that the carnataur had left and I was actually able to finally start doing some collecting materials to craft stuff and actually built a little house on the beach. Contrast that with No Man's Sky where I spawned on a radioactive world but had a nice tutorial prompting me to collect sodium for my hazard protection. That worked quite well as I even got prompted to find a cave when a radioactive storm cropped up. I didn't find a cave until the storm was ending but I had collected enough sodium (and was collecting more while looking for a cave) that I survived quite nicely. I fixed up the ship and didn't actually get killed until like the 5th or 6th world when I got struck by lightning. Overall I died more times in the first 10 minutes of ARK than I did in the first 100 HOURS of NMS......

So I really don't consider NMS to be difficult from a survival aspect at least on normal settings. I'm not eager to try it on the more difficult ones because I'm a bit of a pack rat and keep having to juggle inventory as is without having the limitations on inventory the harder settings give you...... And yes I have all 10 storage containers setup on the freighter so have access to those anywhere I can summon the freighter in and have 2 haulers with 48 slots each right now and a 38 slot fighter and a 35 slot explorer........ So yes. I am a bit of a pack rat........

Everytime an update comes out I try to give this game another shot and every time I walk away empty handed.

This games artstyle and procedurally generated worlds are genuinely gorgeous which makes for great screenshots and trailers - and is probably what will draw a lot of people in. That and that the developers easily could've taken the money and ran but instead chose to stay with the game and provide free updates, which they certainly deserve credit for. 

What most people don't realize however, is that the majority of the content adding is supplemental and does not change the core gameplay loop which is incredibly shallow. Yes, you can now buy a freighter, do some fetch quests, build a base, and explore abandoned ships, but the core gameplay driving it all consists of traveling to a planet, mining resources, making something so you can mine even more resources, mine those resources, run out of fuel, refuel, travel to another planet, and repeat so that you can get as many meaningless credits as possible to spend on a new ship so you can mine even more things. It's as tedious to read as it is to play. 

As a sandbox game apart from discovering new planets, there's aren't enough tools given to the player to construct genuinely interesting or exciting things that feel worthwhile. As a survival game there is nothing to work towards, no challenge, no sense of progression, no endgame, and no mastery over your environment. 

Kudos to the devs for sticking with it but I sincerely hope they place their energy elsewhere, as right now this game makes for better wallpapers than memorable experiences.
