Reviews.113149:
[b]VR Only Review[/b]:
TL;DR summary right at the top: I haven't and won't play this game without VR, so this review may not be relevant to everyone. As VR games go, this one is pretty good with a few caveats. Were this not a VR game I would pan it and tell people not to buy it in 2021 for being way too shallow. However, with the VR market for games being so thin as a VR purchase I do recommend it- on sale. Don't pay full price for this.

1. [b]Base Building and Resources[/b]: The construction and resource gathering being the first mechanic you're introduced to are very shallow. The buildings do leave quite a bit to be desired and to use the easy comparisons is not a mine craft or space engineers competitor.

1a. The plants and minerals are extremely repetitive. Everything boils down to the same elements like carbon for example, but that doesn't mean things need to look so similar in a game that pitches itself as mostly an exploration game. Though every time you touch down on a planet everything you look at is "unique" to that planet things follow a super obvious template so much so that the plants and rocks really don't strike any significant differences. 

1b. The only significant differences are between planet types such as a ice bound planet or a fiery planet. These overarching types dictate the lighting effects on a planet, and the types of plants / mineral templates it'll use, but one fiery planet is very, very, very similar to the next.

2. [b]Animals[/b]: The animals are pretty wacky. Mostly in a good way. I haven't been disappointed by  the animals, they seem to have a larger template to create from and can be pretty unique. The AI on these animals virtually non-existent but I can't say I've ever run across a particularly intelligent squirrel in real life so this shortcoming doesn't really break too much for me.

3. [b]The space flight is excellent.[/b] Especially as a VR experience. This is the part of the game that keeps me coming back. There are likely better flight sim games, but this game does strike a pretty good balance between the fun of flying and the in-game utility of it. [i]Protip when flying in VR: Don't focus on where you're aiming. Fly by feel like you do when you drive a car or ride a bike. Look where you want to go and then just start turning the ship- you'll get it. It takes a bit to get used to but swinging a spaceship around feels natural once you start ignoring the aiming piper. Because of how natural this feels is actually the reason I recommend the game.[/i]


4. [b]AI Lifeforms[/b]: The other AI sentient life forms leave a metric boat load to be desired. Not much good can be said other than they do serve to make the universe seem less empty. They don't do anything other than stand around and work as set dressing or a way to grind stuff that as far as I can tell you don't really need to do for anything other than bragging points.

5. [b]Other players[/b]:You don't run into other people unless you invite them or go to one of the two (that I'm aware of) instanced space stations in the whole universe. To put that in context, every star system has a space station just about meaning there are hundreds of thousands of them, if not millions or billions. But these two stations are not super important places to go. You'll spend far more time in the super repetitive non-instanced space stations that you will not see a person in. I won't list this as a pro or a con, that is up to the individual.

6. [b]Performance[/b]: I run this on a i9 with a GeForce 2080 Super with 8 gigs of VRAM. Even disabling every other application, cutting my desktop resolution down and disabling my second screen I cannot run this game on anything but "enhanced" settings which are 2 out of 4 on the sliders. I can run Half Life Alyx maxed out easily. Having done some research I can't find anyone "flexing" saying they are maxing it out. It does run smooth enough turned down to enhanced but I wouldn't describe the game as eye candy at that level.

6a. [b]Nausea Notes[/b]: Everyone experiences VR nausea differently and I've yet to meet an honest person who says they never get it. The game is either playable smoothly, or just unplayable so that is nice enough that you can't get it wrong. Once I go beyond enhanced (mentioned above) the game gets too framey to be played at all even if I swapped to a mouse/keyboard combo. But at enhanced it is smooth enough that the laggyness that causes nausea is non-existent typically. [b]But and this is a massive but, all of the loading screens are nightmares of tunnel zooming flashy animations.[/b] I've learned to just close my eyes during any and all loading screens otherwise your session will likely be cut short after looking at enough of them.
Reviews.113150:
The most legendary comeback story in gaming. Plagued by poor deadlines, a small and inexperienced staff, and expectations that eclipsed even the inconceivably large, procedurally generated world the game advertised, this game had one of the most disappointing launches in gaming history. But unlike many other comparable botched launches, No Man's Sky's was redeemed. Years later and with a truly respectable, dedicated team remaining at the helm, No Man's Sky is now a flourishing, deep, and massive game that is nearly unrecognizable from it's first release. It's still getting updates to this day; massive, significant updates, including the addition of animal taming and breeding (which at the time of writing this, was just added a few days ago!), a fully-fledged VR mode, and many, many other additions that make this game the massive space sandbox game it was always meant to be.

But if the game's development is a great and inspiring story, how is the game itself? Well, if I had a word to use to describe the whole game, it would be immersive. Everything in the game works together to transport you, the player, to the far-off and exotic locations of the game, and to give you the ability to interact with this world in a spectacular way. Your first visits to a space station will be awkward and esoteric, but once you begin picking up the languages of the aliens, you learn bits of their history, their feelings, and their motivations. Eventually, you can make sense of the world around you, but this is a long and arduous journey from the start of the game, where you are stranded on a random planet with no idea of how or why you're there, or who you are, or what anyone is doing. That feeling of discovery surrounds every aspect of the game, and though there have been many players before and will be many players after you, it still feels like everything you do and everywhere you go is new, uncharted, and untamed.

I highly recommend this game to anyone who wants to feel that discovery. Especially if you have a VR headset, because with a good rig this game's VR mode cranks the atmosphere and fun up to 11.

The only time I will ever consider writing a review is when by breath was taken away by the game or when it is really terrible (pubg lol). This is what I consider when reviewing a game:

2. If it is not a full blown amazing storyline game, what type of endgame elements are there / replayabilty.
3. Gameplay elements
4. Community / Devs involvement and the devs ability to listen to community feedback.

No Man's Sky has a reputation behind it. This review is based on first purchasing it [u] a couple of years [/u] after its initial launch, so I do not have any comments on its initial launch not being as good as the hype around it. 

But I will talk about my experience with the game. I don't recommend the game, but it's one of those "well if it's on a good sale..." type of feelings. I bought it at $30, which was (in retrospect) a bit too high for what I got. But that's okay, anyway, here's why.

The game is centered around you being an explorer. You won't really like this game if you don't have a penchant for (sometimes aimless) curiosity.  However, I dislike the speed of exploration in this game, it felt too slow and at times painstaking. Often instead of exploring, I felt I spent more time watching my life support meter (which [b]always[/b] goes down, even in paradise, https://steamcommunity.com/app/275850/discussions/0/135512133545045597/).  Not to mention you also have several other meters that you [u] regurlarly [/u] have to watch. This game is about survival too, and that's fine. But the point is, that took away from the exploration aspect of the game. They should complement each other, not detract. I never felt [u] motivated [/u] to explore to enhance my survival chances, it felt more like surviving was just a chore. There is a "no survival" game mode, but I didn't want my only options annoying survival or no survival at all.

That, and the slow speed of uneventful, un-engaging harvesting further contributed to this slow, sometimes repetitive, exploration feel. The pacing that I would unlock new structures, or improvement customization also felt too slow. After about 40 hours in, I felt like I wasn't really having fun yet, but was putting in work so I could have fun later. Then I realized, that's a lot like what a work week is, so I put this game down and actually started having fun.

The story and missions are there, they help guide you, and it's fine. It's not bad, but it's not that exciting. The game does have positives- the graphics are usually pretty good, the weather effects are cool, the discovery you get from playing the game is somewhat satisfying. The openness that you can really do whatever things you want can be empowering. But I don't want to just target a plant with a laser beam to get Oxygen and then move to the next plant, so I don't recommend this game.

All and all, No Man's Sky is about atmosphere. 

To those looking for more action packed game, No Man's Sky still doesn't have much to offer. Combat exists, but pretty much sticks between the amazingly easy (Pirates and Predators) and the frustratingly overpowered (Endless waves of Sentinels). Questing is mostly limited to the main story (fairly interesting, but a little lonely), building quests and fetch quests. Maybe more updates will improve these areas, but as it is, No Man's Sky is (currently) not for those looking for an active gaming experience.

However, to those who want something subtle and sublime, this game has both in spades

Soar across lava fields in your own personal spaceship. Delve into ruins to find long lost species or into infested space hulks to make your way pasts hordes of aliens and survive either to win priceless treasures. Stand on airless wastelands looking up at the stars above you. Find a weird critter on a strange planet, name it, ride it and turn it into your personal mount. Learn an alien language.  Build a space-station. The experience of No Man's Sky is always a little bit quiet and a bit transcendent. 

Hopefully we'll see the RPG and combat elements expanded on in the future. Until then it's still a great experience, that I'd recommend to anyone who just simply loves the feel of exploration and find strange and fantastic worlds.

There are pluses. You can build your own base(s). Did not realize that a base got 'grown over' if you wander too far or don't visit it regularly. A sub-part of that is a plus though if you put a base next to a crashed ship...you get to reclaim it multiple times. Another plus is the fact that you get to fly a ship and have space battles. After a while though the space battles can get a little boring. Landing on a derelict freighter can be interesting for the first few times, until you realize the fight through those are also the same unless you 'switch' planetary systems.
Tl;dr? If you want to constantly farm a ton of different resources and spend thousands of hours flying through the galaxy to the end?...good luck with that. Wanna build a base?...farming the resources or the money to get the resources will take a long time. Space battles are cool. Other than that....meh.

Despite a rough launch, this game actually has a lot to offer now. If you enjoy exploration/survival games, No Man's Sky has a lot to offer, and has received amazing post-launch support and is still getting better. As of the latest update, there's significant base building, player-owned capital ships and fleets, OPTIONAL coop multiplayer (can still easily play offline if desired which is a huge plus for me), and a host of other features.

However, there are some fundamental flaws (IMHO) with the core game design that are so deeply baked in that I don't see them really being able to changed without drastically changing the game itself.
First off, the procedural generation is a double edged sword. Its neat that there's for all practical purposes an infinite number of systems to visit each with "unique" life, but the reality is that once you've seen one or two of each planet archetype you've pretty much seen them all, same thing goes for the procedurally generated flora and fauna, and the ships and multitools.

Diving deeper into the ships and multitools, for some inexplicable reason there's no way to customize their appearance, you can't even change the color. The game wants to waste your time making you go from system to system until you find one with an appropriate seed to generate what you want. The latest update just added the ability to customize creatures and breed your own with the ability to choose how they look, but frustratingly this feature is still completely MIA for tools and ships despite it being MORE logical to be able to do it for them than for creatures. Hopefully a future update will rectify this, but for now its a baffling omission.

The second massive flaw is inventory management. A lot of games do this poorly, and No Man's Sky takes it even further. The vast majority of my time is spent with the un-fun task of constantly juggling inventory, and even when building a base inventory space is shockingly limited to 200 slots max. To add insult to injury, the amount of storage ships have is often less than your backpack, and ship prices are based on storage more than anything else. Inventory capacity upgrades are few and far between, limited to just one upgrade per system, and even more limited for ships with needing to scrap ships for a chance to get one or finding rare crash sites. In other words, a huge amount of the game progression is based around limiting player inventory which is just awful game design IMHO. Once you've built everything you want to build it largely goes away since you can dedicate those slots to just the fuel and resources you need to travel, but early game is really, really rough on this front with needing to gather resources for all the things you need to build but constantly running out of space, wasting a bunch of time juggling all that to get everything built. Not much fun IMHO.

Overall I can recommend this game due to the amazing post-launch support and the large amount of content, but be aware that this game does have significant flaws which make it a lot more frustrating and tedious at times than it needs to be.

Edit: After having played more and run into more and more frustration with the inventory and progression systems, I can safely say that this game is best played in creative mode. Survival mode is just a grind and time sink more than anything else that's largely unsatisfying after the first few hours.

Edit: After having finished the "story" (or what passes for it in this game) and experienced a lot of tedium and repetition even with all the benefits of creative mode, I've unfortunately decided to not recommend this game. I recognize that the devs have made tremendous improvements to the game since launch and they should definitely be applauded for that, but even with all the improvements there's still a LOT of rough edges and bugs, a deeply unsatisfying "universe is a simulation and nothing actually matters" "story", and some fundamental flaws with the procedural generation and gameplay loops that ultimately make the game not much fun to play in the long run.

For a certain type of player (coop base building, chill flying/walking around in a sci-fi setting) this game isn't bad, but I have a hard time recommending it to players who enjoy games like Empyrion Galactic Survival and similar games since No Man's Sky is just so shallow on nearly everything.

When No Man's Sky hit, amidst all the hype, the reviews were mediocre. Multiplayer wasn't really there, content was minimal... the game clearly wasn't ready. At the time, I thought "I'll give it five years, maybe then it will be ready."

Well, five years later, multiplayer exists, there's lots more content and... the game still isn't good. It's somewhat technically impressive in the visual variety the planets offer, but the gameplay doesn't rise to that level of diversity. Bugs abound, and features are poorly polished -- co-op multiplayer is very limited, base building is awkward, and a large amount of time is spent gathering the same resources to refill the same suit/ship stores. Even when "progressing" it's mostly blowing up slightly different rocks which produce differently named inventory clutter so you can progress further down a technology tree of yawn-worthy upgrades.

The story is... present.

Overall, a cool demo of a vast universe of samey, empty places to slowly grind your way through the periodic table.

After playing for a while i started to notice how limiting everything was Keep in mind this is based solely on the Vanilla aspect no mods. 
-Main Critique
-The planets feel too small especially when digging takes 10 seconds to get to the bottom of the planet. 
-Nothing to do on these planets other then make a base that doesn't really have much going for it you have a couple things to build in the base that are functional but most of the resources are used for building rooms and not really putting anything in them. 
-Every time i go to a new planet it is because i wanted to complete a mission and never revisit the planet again. Should add more unique items to planets that make it stand out compared to others. Sure you have tons of galaxies to explore but there isn't much in those said galaxies because all the planets look the same. 

-Suggestions 
-Having interchangeable parts for your spaceship creating more unique looks 
- add more unique base items that increase crafting capabilities
-Orbital bases or creating custom space stations would be a really neat addition because all of the space stations are identical aside from the local items and shape that they appear outside. 
-I really enjoy the concept of underwater bases but that is all very limiting considering how the vertical glass tunnel does not connect with any of the other tunnels which had huge potential but that is just 1 thing of many 
-docking the nautilon to snap to your base and landing it would have been another nice addition. 
-add more sea creatures to water planets it feels very empty especially some predators
-increase the depth of how far you can go into planets whether deeper underwater or underground
-Allow building on freighters
-Increase unique resources for planets to have a reason to go to them other than buying it from the terminal
-add unique cities in planets would add a more unique feel to visiting a galaxy 

-Bugs
There are also some very glaring bugs that exist 4 years later such as clipping through buildings unintentionally and getting pushed out from a area when trying to dig up items. 

I leave it as recommended because as it does get limiting I was able to enjoy it for a while and hopefully come back to it in the future when they add more big updates.

"No mans sky is good now" my ass

Playing no mans sky, at least in the first 10 or so hours, is just flying/running around planets collecting the same resources and going to several, mostly desolate, locations.

Exploring isn't interesting because all of the early planets have the same stuff on them and can be boiled down to a few different planet types. Finding flora and fauna is about as interesting as seeing a different colored fern.

Flying around in a ship is boring, essentially just going from a to b. The devs thought it would be a great idea if they made it take 1-3 minutes to travel between planets, so have fun going afk. Space fights are very shallow and mining asteroids is a boring as it is in any other space game(Avorion sucks ass).

The graphics are a very mixed bag even on max due to procedural generation. Some planets will look great, others like Spore(2008). This is due to some combinations of sun intensity, ground textures, and weather effects not combining well.

This game is still under heavy development, and features are being added about every other month at the current rate.  Like all survival games it follows the same basic primus: gather resources, build stuff, sell stuff, upgrade stuff. This biggest thing to do in this game is hunt the perfect ship and then upgrade the crap out of it… for no other reason then to have a nice ship that has had the crap updated out of it. Graphics are awesome, game is interesting, and new features are fun to explore.

But… let’s keep it real. This is where I mention the not so good for those wondering if they should buy it. The game suffers from the same problems all survival open-world, open-ended games suffer from: Nothing to do once you finished the story and got the perfect ship and your base is rocking, and you have wiped out the Universe… uh literally. You eventually become a multi-trillionaire hording massive amounts of resources and dominating the world. Nothing left to do but start over, but this time with one hand tied behind your back.

Time-gating missions and forcing super-low unrealistic resource gathering rates to make it take longer to build or buy things are lazy game development practices to make up for a lack of real content. Example:

Dev- “Here is a piece of the living ship, come back in 22 hours and we will hunt the next piece.” 
Me- “Why? Does finding the next piece require this piece?” 
Dev- “No, but the real time to complete this entire mission is like 45 minutes, and we want to claim its 88 hours of immersive game play.” 
Me- “Oh, so you suck at game progression design then, and don’t want to bother with developing new content to fill in that time!” 
Dev- “Yeah, pretty much.”
Me- “Gottcha. Last question. What game should I go play and get more invested in while waiting 22 hours for yours to let me proceed?”

And now for the truly ugly! The procedural design of the solar systems and planets. Every planet in their universe now has impossibly high mountains. I am talking a tectonic plate shifting brawl. Okay not every planet...but most of them! They use noise to create terrain. Ever seen one of those graphs showing audio noise on a flat plane.. yep that is exactly what they do. Its ridiculous. Good luck finding a nice piece of flat ground to build on. 

Dev- “We gave you a terrain manipulator for your mutli-tool so you could flatten the ground.” 
Me-“Cool!” – log in next day to your base buried in the mountain you flattened – “What happened?”
Dev- “The timer on your terrain manipulation expired. It’s a feature to help fill in all the holes you leave behind when digging up buried technology.” 
Me- “But my base is built here.” 
Dev- “Yeah, you shouldn’t use the terrain manipulator to flatten ground for a base.” 
Me- “Then what do I use it for?” 
Dev-“Immersive gameplaying hours of fun!!!” 
Me-“I just dug a hole with it; hop in!”

The colors or colours (for those of you across the pond) of the world are interesting but can be a little off putting at times. I mean can we please get some more normal blue water, blue sky, green grass planets with flat-ish ground. You know .. earth like. I dig the pink sky, blue grass, yellow water scenes as much as the next person but random colors in the same solar system?

Me-- "Is that a lake of piss?"
Dev-- "No its just yellow water, although this is a toxic planet."
Me-- "That's a lake of piss."
Dev-- "Its not!"
Me-- "There are giant brown turds floating in that lake of piss!"
Dev-- "Yeah, that's not what we intended here."

Anyway, thank god for mods! You must mod this game. Bottom line, point of fact. The very first annoyance you will encounter is selecting anything…. Your cursor has to do a slow circle to commit to it… no kidding it takes 2.5 seconds to just select something. Okay, its like 1 second... but it feels like 2.5 seconds!!! Its like watching the slow progression of the loading icon each time you want to select something… including getting into your ship and dialogue. Oh and that brings me to the next little gem of annoying game design meant to extend the hours of fun and excitement you will encounter, which is watching… every… word… get… spelled… out… on… a… dialogue… screen… when… talking… to… a…. npc. 

Me- “While this Gek is getting his next sentence out, do I use the terrain manipulator or advanced mining laser to blow my freaking head off right now?”
Dev- “Use, the boltcaster.” 
Me- “I got a new game for ya. It’s called “Smack-A-Dev”.”

Thankfully there are mods that can pretty much do any and everything. And when they break, you just can’t stand to play on in vanilla. So you must mod the game for your own sanity. Nexus mods!!! And while you are waiting for those mods to be updated to the new game version you go write a Steam review for the game.

So yeah, the game is fun, and interesting, and graphically its nice. Its not on par with Elite Dangerous, but then again, I don’t think its meant to be. It does what it does, and its fun to play… modded. But hopefully they continue to develop more real content and continue to make the game better so fewer mods are required.  But I say buy it. Add it to your collection. Check it out.

Pretty fun game for a while, but the further you get the more you find the game riddled with bugs and poor design choices. Plenty of room to exploit and plenty of set backs due to bugs. I've had the terrain I modified regenerate and consume my base repeatedly, I've fallen through the ground and died—having my inventory deleted as a result—and my friends playing with me have encountered more serious glitches such as their bases up and disappearing entirely or quest npcs getting bugged and having the main story get stuck forever.

All that sucks, and what makes it worse is that this game has a lot of good things going for it. Building is pretty fun until it breaks. Solar system feels big and fun to explore. It's largely a good game, but the bugs ruin it. It's been out for over four years and that can only lead me to believe that either the devs don't really care about making it a polished game, don't have the resources since it's so old, or it's built so heavily on spaghetti code that they are actually unable to fix some of these issues because the amount of work involved is too much. I want to believe the latter, but none of those are really good.

Despite all the fun I've had, gonna give it a downvote for now since the past, present, and future of this game look pretty bleak.

Reviews.113831:
I purchased this game in 2021, so I don't have any context on what the game started out like or how its improved.  However, I heard about it, and it prompted me to give it a shot.

Pros:
I've played a little under 20 hours, and feel like I've barely scratched the surface in a lot of ways.
For a game that came out almost 5 years ago now, it still looks good.  Some of the age shows, but no one would call it ugly.
The terrain tool is a fantastic mechanic that lets a buggy game have leeway to be buggy (cant get stuck), and its fun to boot
There is enough incentive to make exploration fun, not counting resource gathering

Cons that I can live with:
The creatures are pretty buggy with regard to terrain interaction, which takes from the immersion frequently
The resource gathering loop is repetitive and not terribly rewarding
Some mechanics in the game are not obvious and weren't explained to me even after 20 hours of play, such as starship purchasing (you have to go to a station and talk to other ship captains on the landing floor)

The Dealbreaker (THIS IS FIXABLE, READ THE UPDATE BELOW):
The save system is flawed.  The game has a tendency to crash every few hours or so, which isn't necessarily that bad.  But when you have only very limited opportunities to save in a game meant for exploration, those crashes hurt your desire to explore.  That threat of losing progress and having to redo what was genuine discovery the first time makes this game unplayable in the way that it was designed to be played.
But the biggest flaw in the save system, and one that turned a "maybe would recommend" into a "can't recommend", is the inability of the game to ensure you successfully save even after initiating the process.  Basically, if you hit a save point, but don't wait a minute for it to go through the animation and say it saved, you can lose progress by quitting too quickly.  It does warn you, but if you're trying to exit the game quickly for any reason, its easy to hit the button before you see and comprehend that you just lost the last 20 minutes.  I have played a ton of games with limited save options, but every single one of them ensures that the save completes before letting you do something that would lose progress.  A lot will just prevent you from doing anything while they are saving, but even the ones that don't will still delay exiting until the save process has finished.

UPDATE: As someone pointed out to me, there are pieces of technology that you can research (save points and save beacons) that allow you to craft your own save device on the fly anywhere, and carry them with you.  And those devices save basically instantly instead of the outpost waypoints that were an issue for me.  The fact that you need to go through the whole deploy/save/collect cycle is still annoying, but at least there's a way to do it.  That, combined with the fact that the crashes have been less frequent after playing an additional 60 hours (a few new games, so it might have been something to do with the first system I was in, but ymmv) turn my "No, because" into a "Yes, but".

TL;DR This is a decent game, but a mixed bag to be sure.  The grind for resources is annoying at best, but upgrades eventually make this less of an issue.  Make sure you follow the intro story line at least until you reach (very mild spoiler) [spoiler]The Anomaly[/spoiler].  You need the tech available there to make this a productive playing experience, so be forewarned.  Also, the story line itself presents you with a lot of mystery that isn't explained until way later, but don't waste a ton of time feeling like you fucked up.  Just make sure you craft some Base Teleport Modules at your bases as early as you can.  Don't want to spoil anything, so that's all I'll say.

Also, the Terrain Manipulator has a size adjustment, which on the PC is the R/T keys.  Really annoying that this wasn't listed on the bottom as a control like most of the other context hud displays.  Just know that smaller means more resources overall, but takes longer.

Disregard most of my previous review below. Turns out lag problems were my own (gpu temperatures skyrocketing causing throttling)! So now that I know it actually runs I recommend the game if you can get it at a reasonable price. 

l don't know about long term value/playability but it's worth several hours of inoffensive fun and the developers seem interested in keeping the game fresh and updated, so that's good. 

Bottom line for me is while it is shallow in content and has a few issues here and there, it is pretty and it is fun to spend some time exploring planets with a friend building bases.

----------------------------------------------------------

This is a difficult game to review.

I want to recommend it to everybody. I want so badly to say that everybody should run out and get it.
The thing is: I really, really, really want to play this game because it is super fun and gorgeous. Unfortunately, for me, the game is almost unplayable. 

97% of the time, my game play experience is as follows: everything runs fine for 4 seconds, game/computer freezes completely for 4 seconds, runs fine for 4 seconds, freezes completely for 4 seconds...rinse and repeat. It is the most frustrating and annoying experience imaginable. I know how much fun the game can be because it has worked flawlessly a few times - at least once for a couple hours. The game would be super fun if it worked.

My son bought it for me for Christmas so we can play together (he's on a PS4) but it's too painful. By the way, when I'm glitching and lagging, he can see it - he can see my player stuttering desperately across the beautiful planetary vistas.

With update to date everything update to date (drivers, game etc.) and no other programs running that is my experience.

It is not my system:
Running on 64-bit Windows 10, 32GB ram, GTX 1070, SSD (Alienware 15 R3). System is optimized. All other games work fantastically.

None of the troubleshooting steps from the website or found elsewhere on the internet work. Some appear to work when the game is first loaded but within seconds to minutes the lagging/freezing hell starts up again. I can't shake the feeling that it is some memory allocation issue - like there is some custom garbage collection process that goes off the rails, or perhaps the terrain generation process runs to frequently or something...I dunno. I've tried fixing all the various settings in the xml file to no avail. This has nothing to do with setting the graphics settings too high - the same thing happens if I run at the lowest resolution possible with all graphics settings at lowest setting, windowed/fullscreen.
When it happens, whole computer seems to freeze - if I've alt-tabbed out to the desktop, everything still freezes even though the game is not focused. I played with task manager open and I don't see any spikes in cpu/memory/disk/network when it happens, but as I say the whole computer seems to seize up for the 4 seconds so who knows...

It will say I put a lot of hours in and I have played for several - it's just that most of that playtime has been suffering. Also, my hours are inflated because several times I've just walked away from the computer and left it running all night without quitting the games so it seems like I've played more that I have, but I have put in many hours into the game.

Bottom line, I really want to play this game - it is really quite enjoyable. I understand the developers have put in a lot of effort since release to make it special. It just seems like there is some fundamental issue wrong still that they haven't got a hold of - my experience points to some fundamental bug/issue that has yet to be fixed and it makes the game almost completely unplayable. I've powered through it several times because the game is actually very fun but it's really not a good experience in any way.

I do have other issues/complaints with the game (e.g. network/friend play has some kinks yet) but if this lag/freeze issue were to be fixed (I would be so interested to hear what the underlying problem is) then this game would be a definite buy recommendation from me. It really is fun and very, very beautiful. As it is however, I cannot recommend due to the technical issues I've faced.

Reviews.113978:
I wasn't there for the controversy - I started playing in 2021. All I know is that the game as it exists today is superb. 

Over the last 110 hours, I've discovered hundreds of alien worlds in some capacity, and gotten a good personal look at many of them. I've made many bases, from my first pile of wood on a green irradiated ball of weeds, to a preexisting trade tower on a paradise planet that I took over and made many additions to, to the first time I built a real, proper, organized shelter from scratch with every amenity, on the most freezing, stormy ice world I've ever seen. I felt so powerful, knowing I'd made my own little paradise in the wilderness. I've been to worlds recommended by friends and the online NMS community, containing all sorts of wonders, from beautiful ships, to unique fauna that happen to have procedurally generated to be adorable, to giant works of art and ingenuity made by other players. I've finished the story, which was heartbreaking and quite high quality, and then traveled to the next galaxy after the already impossibly large first one. I've met people and done missions together. I've been gifted money and items by the hugely generous community, including an egg, which I then hatched. Now I have my companion for life - a living ship, and I adore her. She's such a blast to fly around killing pirates with.

There are some problem areas. There are lots of bugs, for starters. The gear ladder is currency based, and not as tall as you'd expect, so if you manage to become filthy rich via some clever way like indium farming, you can rob yourself of a lot of content. On the flip side of that, the base building progression system is actually pretty slow and tedious, requiring you to collect a lot of one specific item, so it takes a while to fully unlock your Minecrafting potential. This is weird, since it seems like the difficulty levels should be the other way round - surely you want anyone to be able to make a great base to express themselves artistically, but gear should be tricky?

This is all pretty well fixed by the fact that you can make your save file in any one of four gamemodes. If progression is too easy, make a survival save. If base building progression is too hard, make a creative save. If you really just want punishment, or the biggest challenge of all, play permadeath. Otherwise, normal. It's not a perfect balance fix - creative means that save file can never experience challenge even if it wants to, which is limiting, and due to the high bug density, a permadeath run can easily just fail because you clipped through a planet and suffocated in the ground. But it's good the options are there, and I'll definitely be trying a permadeath run myself soon.

In the end, the real reason this game is wonderful is the community, and the way that provides the perfect ambiance. The universe is massive and empty, and unless you seek them out, you'll probably never meet another soul... it's total isolation, but in a world where other people are out there somewhere, which feels really interesting. Then, though, if you do seek others out, you'll find the Galactic Hub, and NMS Coordinates Exchange, and hang out at the Anomaly, and suddenly it's a thriving MMO with full player control of how the universe is settled and built upon. And everyone is so, so friendly. I think that's because it's such a massive, empty universe - when you're dropped in a place like this, your natural instinct is to share, and explain, and direct, because if nobody does, we'll all be alone. As much as it's a game about loneliness, it's a game about the natural human drive to want to find life among nothing, and form any bond they can. It's about reaching out and making friends.

I can't recommend this game enough. You'll get your money's worth somewhere in this universe, be it in the time spent with others in community areas, the challenges of combat, the creative expression of a really intuitive base building system, or the silent joy of standing on a paradise world with rolling pink fields, watching the bouncing smiley snakes graze.

This game gets better the more you play it. Explore,craft and survive. Exploration is pretty amazing , you can travel all over space meeting different lifeforms from flying cows to two legged goats The planets are great canvass to build on and you can shape the ground with tools later on in the game.
 The creatures in the game are cool but I feel more variety is needed and some of the coolest creatures are rarely spawned such as the long necked dino types which you won`t find unless you are very lucky. They are spawns from templates with a few tweaks to  keep them unique.  The creatures are not very fierce  you won`t be matched subnautica style  creatures that attack your ship which I found disappoint but hey you can feed creatures and freaking ride them including two legged goats! .
Crafting is fun and gathering for crafting is really fun but like a lot of things in this game its something you will explore a few hours into game but I have yet to embrace this part of the game properly so I cannot comment too much on it.
This game does have mods nothing like elder scrolls but the modding community is growing despite it having a few co-op multiplayer elements the game is  not competitive and  directed toward visiting other players bases so modding the game isnt frowned upon. Sadly some mods  are outdated  and many get abandoned so don`t get your hopes up too much. They have mods to make creature scanning easier but I am yet could not find any good overhaul creature mods in date. =(
The game has a story and missions which are important for unlocking new tools  to get the most out of the game. I quite like it.
The races in the game are awesome and the language system in the game is insanely good! You can unlock new words by finding knowledge stones but even funner is unlocking new words by talking to aliens  asking them to help you and  trying to talk to them using their lang and improve your standing with their race. Using some words with some races will offend them so you need to get to know each one and their lang.You can also give them gifts to improve standing with them but only fixed gifts they like.
Survival is good but it isn`t The Long Dark good , the focus isnt on food and drink but life support and protection from the elements. Some planets are harsher than others and you`ll be shooting your miner gun for oxygen and carbon a lot. The game stack slots are great.
The economy  in nomansky is awesome  , you`ve got nanites you get for scanning and naming creatures , fixing machines etc and you,ve got units you get from trading and doing missions. I found these both satisfying. You also have quicksliver you get doing missions in other player,s world which youcan spend on new skins.
Overall very fun game just wish there where more creatures and better creature AI. Thats the biggest flaw for me the rest of the game is great and I`m glad I bought it, I don`t play many space exploration games but this one was fun if somebody combined nomanysky with community creature editing (spore style) and topped it off with improved creature ai this game would be near perfect for me but as it is it is still tons of fun and worth playing (=  .

I've played for long enough to conclude that it's just a horrible, tedious game where the biggest challenge is managing your tiny inventory and fetching materials in order a get the materials you need to get other materials so that you can stay alive, fly your ship, power your mining device etc. There is no fun in any of the challenges. I tried really hard to get into it and enjoy it but then I needed to go get 100 copper for something and I just thought "I don't want to". Getting copper isn't fun. I need to mine crystals to power my ship then scan planets then trudge around until I find some and then load it into some device to power it up so I can go find more materials. I've only had to engage in combat twice and it was easy, quick and meaningless. Even the complex and clunky menus are a hideous boundary between the player and good time. Some interface elements require a long click, some require a long press of "E" right-click is nearly a universal "back" button - "Esc" backs out of some things. It's a mess. A boring, tedious mess where your biggest, most challenging enemies are your own inventory and the horrific user interface.

No Man's Sky taught the video game industry a bunch of important lessons but none of them were ones that anyone would want to emulate. The first is to not promise something you can't deliver - the hype will be based on the promise and the disappointment will haunt you forever. The second is that infinite content doesn't make for an interesting experience. There are billions of planets to be bored and frustrated on in No Man's Sky. Consider the first Borderlands - one fixed, barren planet but teaming with things to do; that's a game. Infinite variation in the shapes and colours of a boring wasteland is not a game so much as a tech demo.

Also if you open a chest with a full inventory, the valuable item inside just vanishes with no way to get it back and you inventory is ALWAYS accidentally full.

Why do I love this game? 
It's got so much to explore. So much to craft, so much to take, so much to see. So much to colonize and so much to build. 
I first played this game on PS4 I had gone through many adventures with this game. It was not without its ups and downs. I preordered No Man's Sky the moment I got my chance it was why I bought a PS4 and now it is why I built a gaming PC! 

I used to think we will never ever be able to get a game that can make you feel like you're in Star Trek. The universe is too big sure, open world games come out all the time throughout the year. 

But this was my first taste of an "open UNIVERSE" game! Yes, it crashed, it had bugs and glitches but it was still fun. I still remember when bases had a complexity limit and you could only build and base spots within a bubble. 

It sucked I had to lose my base after an update. And yes I once created an overly wild project that caused the whole area to glitch and it would crash within 3 seconds upon starting th game. 

I had over 500 hours in that sad file. I had no choice but to delete it and start anew. Universal resets were also problematic causing bases to appear underneath the ground or tropical planets to become frozen hellholes. It was sad to experience those but I learned from the and kept on progressing! 

Now it's time to join the PC master race! It was totally worth buying the game again.
It is interesting that while PC and PS4 gets constant updates, however the PS4 suffers from too much environmental loading and pop-in. 

I am aware that there is the PS5 I could have gone from the PS4 to the PS5. But as consumer I saw signs of a changing Playstation (brand). I don't think I can get behind that platform anymore. 

Even when the PS5 was just rumors I had "zero" excitement for the PS5 + the momentum was being ruined by scalpers. 

I did get the chance to pick up a PS5 controller though and pair it to my PC. For most games my preferred way to play will still be on controller I will only use the mouse and keyboard for certain situations or the games that require it. 

So far I feel like it is very comfortable to play NMS on PC with a PS5 controller I highly recommend getting one if you can find one. 

I love the fully packed button mapping functionality that Steam has to offer and let's me move around or copy and paste from game to game if they allow it. 

I can make it an easier button to press instead of control+shift and whatever it is because I keep forgetting the third one I have to press at the same time and that is annoying! 

The button scheme on PC if you're playing on a PS4 controllers or PS5 hasn't changed at all from how you would play on the actual console unless you change it. 

No Man's Sky is definitely a game worth buying multiple times if you are that type of person. 

Happy gaming and have a great joy ride in space!

From how it was at launch, this is a pretty good game, but it still needs a lot of work, there's unneeded restrictions on some things, there's not a lot of variety in others, and it still doesn't match what it promised around 4 years ago.

This game restricts you in a lot of different places, timers in quests and ship collection are two major ones. Timers are in a lot of places in this game. Crafting stations have them, quests have them, and even exploration has them (albeit they're shorter than the others). Crafting stations are different from the normal inventory crafting, but they are still important. It takes sometimes up to minutes for things to be made in crafting stations which just feels like a lazy way to stretch out content sometimes. Quests can have multiple hour long timers in them. For instance I was doing a quest for a korvax I hired to come to my base and there were at least two hour long timers in that quest. The quest for living ships was riddled with them, because first you would have to get the egg with 3200 quicksilver (I'll get to that later) and then fly around until the quest starts, once it does, the whole quest is just "go to x coordinates and find y" then "gather z and make a" and finally once you make a and give it to y you're given a new item that needs to mature for usually ~24 hours. I just changed the time on my computer because I'm not waiting a week to get a ship that doesn't even have the best stats. This quest was actually awful. Exploring usually has around a 30 second timer whenever you go between planets, I get they're a long distance apart, but it's not engaging to look at my ship fly closer to a planet for 30 seconds. Collecting ships isn't as big of a problem, but it's still a pretty major one. You can only have six ships at any given time. As of now there are 6 classes of ships (hauler, explorer, exotic, living, fighter, and shuttle) which that sounds fair, but there's different models and parts on the ships that make each one unique (or as unique as possible). There are currently three living ship models, so if you wanted to have one of each model, you would be taking up half of your ship collection just on living ships.

For having an ever expanding universe with close to infinite planets, there's surprisingly little variety in how you play the game. Most of the weapons are bad and the full inventory of a properly modded multi tool can only support two fully upgraded ones, which only one is really good anyway. There's not even any variety on how you mod anything other than your weapons, because there isn't different types of anything other than weapons. So you always end up the same way even trying to be different. There's three different races in the game and none of them effect close to noticeable anything about game play so there is no real reason to max out your reputation with any of them. It's just a very simple system to figure out.

I don't quite match what they said it did, but I can't really hold a lot against them. My main problems are with fighting in space, sandworms, and animals effecting each other. From the promotional material you see things like two freighters warping in and warring against each other, giving you the ability to choose sides. This never happens, you still see freighters and they do get attacked, but only by pirates and never by any other race. Sandworms are pretty self explanatory, they were supposed to be giant worms that were on desert planets, but they just are not in the game at all. The biggest one I have is that animals do not care for each other, you'd expect on harsh planets that you would constantly see animals fighting each other like they did in the trailers, but no, they just spawn in and wander around or are hostile to you. Animals can be tamed, but they can't be transported so there's no point. 

Overall, the game is really good with major flaws that bring it down. I would recommend waiting for it to go on sale, but other than that, get it. It's a really fun space explorer with plenty of content that give you hundreds of hours of fun.

VR

I love the VR implementation on this game, it's very fitting and for the most part it feels really natural to play (just don't go to laggy bases or anything like that). That being said there's a few problems I have with it. For instance, there's no head tracking, so when you look around, other players see you looking straight forward, as well as the HUD not moving with you. The HUD can also sometimes be in the ground or far away so text can be hard to read, with no way to change it if you are mid-conversation with an NPC. Some races (probably only the gek) also have very short limbs, so with the new full body view it's really hard to tell where your hands are because you'll probably always be reaching ahead of where your character is.

Depends on what you're looking for. I suggest this game predominantly to friends I know, whose kids are getting into PC gaming and that love space things, building games, exploring etc. But to someone who likes space games? In general? Obviously not at all. So let's break this down into Pros and Cons.

Pros
1. Vibrant and exciting worlds teaming with life (95% of the time).
2. Endless exploration, with over 200 galaxies.
3. The most frequent updates I've ever seen in a game and they tend to bring lots to the plate.
4. At the start of the game you can choose your style of play; building/ creator mode, explore, story, survival...
5. Err...interesting(?) ships.
6. Base building
7. Aircraft carriers done right! Take that! Elite Dangerous! 
8. Manage a fleet of capital ships and send them on missions for income and resources...again, "Take that! Elite!" 

Cons
1. Not a flight sim. In fact there are no lateral or vertical motions in this space game (my biggest gripe).
2. All worlds begin to look the same, but each update seems to slightly change that.
3. Hot or cold rain hurts you in an insulated space suit, which should be rated at like +/ - 250 degrees, but? Some how doesn't hurt that cute little creatures frolicking around.
4. Ship designs are not attractive at all...most look like Duplos or Legos.
5. All of the galaxies only have the same 3 main life forms (minus the sentinels and one-off traveler that may appear).
6. Too cartoony.

Absolutely horrible beginning on Survival (Default/Standard) mode.  No explanation, no time to think, large blocks of text/UI to learn while it's blaring "RADIATION PROTECTION FAILING".  You'd love to stop and learn the game, but you aren't able to pause the game on these informative popups, meanwhile the game is screaming at you to hurry up before you die, nice.  So it's telling you to find a "yellow" plant, great, you see a bunch of yellow plants everywhere, but nothing happens when you zap them (oops not *that* yellow plant silly tee hee).  So you die, again and again, then you find this stupid yellow plant after 15 minutes of frantically running around looking for it...and it only gives you another 2 minutes of life before you die again anyway.  

You've now played 30 minutes and have heard "RADIATION PROTECTION FAILING" at least a few hundred times, and as far as you can tell you're going to have to listen to that blaring message indefinitely because your life is going to be running around looking for more yellow plants to refill your radiation protection so that you can live long enough to find more yellow plants.

At this point i uninstalled it.  

3 Months later decided to try one more time.  Got past the opening.  Overall, it would be a fun game but the constant bugs & glitches slowly wear on you.  I just partially solved the extremely late 'terrain pop in' (you'll be running around a mostly-empty looking landscape and suddenly rocks and trees appear near you or even behind you) with a mod, but now am dealing with terrain that I previously terraformed (removed), reappearing INSIDE my base.  

Oh and btw if you die you lose everything on your body, and you have no warning of this at all.  (yes this might be expected in a harder mode, but we're talking the default game mode, and it deletes a potentially devastating amount of stuff you've got on you, at least in the early game).  

I will probably keep playing it some due to something related to the sunk cost fallacy and/or hoping I will slowly get a handle on all the bugs, but I would not recommend this to any off my friends.

Reviews.150213:
You've probably heard about No Man's Sky's awful launch, but honestly? That doesn't matter anymore. Hello Games experienced one of the worst PR fallouts ever, and took it in stride. The game has been updated and cared for with such dedication, it's actually quite good now. Community concerns are regularly reviewed and addressed in updates, the graphics are beautiful, and the game is just fun overall. It's getting to the point that the typical $60 asking price isn't actually unreasonable anymore.

The developers could easily have abandoned this project and tried to move on, but they stuck around through the negativity and have pushed to make this a good game. All updates have been free, so I've gotta say I'm satisfied with my purchase.

As for what the game's actually about, for those not yet aware, No Man's Sky might remind you of Animal Crossing, Elite Dangerous, and a horror-based visual novel all mashed together. There's base building, resource gathering, exploring the galaxy, space combat, questing, storytelling, and some very heavy underlying themes.

Get it while it's still on sale, if you can. You can always return it within 20hrs of gameplay if you're truly unsatisfied, but it's definitely worth a try.

Hello Games have proven to be some of the most dedicated developers in the industry, and have turned this game from one of the most disappointing launches in recent memory, to one of the greatest cross platform games ever made. It will become a classic.


ORIGINAL REVIEW

Note: although I only have a few hours playtime on Steam, I was a PS4 pre-order buyer and racked up many more hours there before making the switch to PC for multiplayer (we have multiple Steam ready machines in the house)

NMS is a great game for fans of exploration and crafting. It's come a hell of a long way since launch, Hello Games have added so much content and tweaked mechanics to a point that I believe we now have the game we were all expecting at launch. Granted, there could still be a lot more variety in planets and creatures and at times you feel like you're just seeing the same things over and over again, but this has improved so much over time I'm sure it will just keep getting better.

Multiplayer is fun, although limited to 4 players (actually 12 per session but only 4 in a party, the remaining 8 players will be 'orbs' rather than full character models). You're free to work together to build bases and share resources, enabling you to get quite a complex production line going to maximise profits as you work towards the ultimate goal (for me and the OH at least) of owning a massive freighter stocked with S-class ships. 

Considering the game is regularly on sale below £20, it's well worth picking up and trying now. Try to forget all the bad press the game got when it launched two years ago. There are still flaws, but HG just keep improving this game with every update. Now is a great time to get in to NMS.

This is by no means a perfect video game but it has come to be one of my favorites, ever. 

 A no-pressure gameplay loop along with casual exploration and wonderous aesthetics bring a pleasant zen experience, for the most part. Things like inventory management and the grind of resource collecting can be a chore, and some gamers won't even find much of a challenge in its most hardcore modes.  

But it's the perfect game for someone like me.  I enjoy the casual nature of it all, from the easy survival elements to the enemies that are tough — but not too tough.  I like exploring more planets than I could comprehend and seeing slight differences in each one until I find a PERFECT planet, one that will TRULY be the one I'll start my base from and move down out of my freighter.  Alas, no, there's always going to be a better planet out there — I just have to find it. 

No Man's Sky is the Cinderella Story of gaming: the launch was nearly catastrophic and reviews everywhere saw the potential of a very, very unfinished game with what some believer were undelivered promises that could not justify a score worth of a full MSRP purchase, or a purchase at all.    Through love and work and communication with its community, Hello Games has turned its botched launch in to a worthy title and one that deserves its spot on the digital shelf of any space exploration gamer.

Warning, this review will contain a fairly large amount of text. I'll try to break it up into key points so that it's easier to digest. My review will reflect my experiences in-game and not the points made by other reviewers. Yes, that is a dig at the huge amount of Steam users piggy backing on negative reviews after a whopping 2.5 hours of play time.

Performance
- I'm running everything at max, I've not had a single wobble, frame drop or glitch that I've noticed. NMS is running as smooth as butter for me, sadly not all Steam users are experiencing the same performance. I really hope we get a patch that fixes this, you're missing out on an awesome game.

Stability
- I've had one crash. I lost an hour of really enjoyable game-play. I expected this, I'm not going to cry and leave a negative review, because, well because I'm not twelve years old. We're playing a game that procedurally generates a universe for us to explore. Expect some issues at launch, release date delays or not. If that's not OK, don't buy it.


Some key points:
An unlimited amount of planetary exploration. Find loot galore, a huge variety of minerals, materials and goodies to hunt.
Animals, creatures, monsters, cute and weird things to hunt, scan, chase, feed or just ignore.
Plenty of upgrades or merchants to buy from: New equipment, weapons and ships.
Great visuals, music, sfx - Very atmospheric.


EDIT - As of my 35 hours in game.
I have exactly 35 hours in game. And I'd like to touch on a few points. Things that I didn't mention in my previous review text, I've enjoyed enough of the game to accurately describe how I feel about NMS.

Exploration after 35 hours
I'm still enjoying exploring. The variation of planets is insane. Sure, the creatures on planets are generated from a massive pool of body parts, so you get giant dinosaur like creatures with thin birdy legs, but why this upsets some users is beyond me. This is a science fiction exploration game not an evolution simulator.

Also, so what, we fall through the creatures when we try to jump on them. I read a review by a man that swings a giant sex toy around that focused on this, saying NMS is like a house of cards.
We can hunt and scan a vast amount of alien creatures in this Universe. Why is it so upsetting that can't ride them? I mean, if you want to ride a dino-alien, go and play Ark. It's awesome.

Planets are so large it's crazy. There are what seems like infinite environmental possibilities too. Exploring different outposts, Monoliths, trade stations, colonial bases, crashed ships and more is still an awesome experience for me, I enjoy searching out weird and wonderful planets. I particularly enjoy planets with insanely harsh or toxic weather. Upgrading my exo-suit to deal with these environments was something I tried to do as early as I could. Cave diving on underwater planets has been so much fun. Mainly when I'm on a planet that is light on Plutonium, I go deep underground to search it out.

Some of the anomalies that I have come across in space have been really cool too. Including black holes, alien space-outposts, Atlas interfaces, weird manufacturing facilities and plenty more. There is so, SO much more to do, more variety and fun to be had than a lot of the neg reviews claim.

Alien life
Interacting with Alien life forms is cool, this is probably my favourite aspect of the game. Find some sort of outpost, building, structure etc - Speak to an alien inside, answer a question or give the alien an item, help the alien with something, or just reply to them in a certain way to receive a reward.
Interacting with the creatures is leaving me feeling like I understand some of the alien races and what they're all about more and more. Of course, you'll find alien life out in the depths of space too. On space stations random ships will dock. You can interact with the pilot from each ship, trade with them and offer to buy their ships.

The story so far
I've also loved following the text narrative that makes up the flesh of the story in No Man's Sky. Another common negative critique I'm reading, is that the game doesn't have a solid story. But I feel it does, you just need to read the text on the screen guys, it's all there.

Combat (On foot and in your ship)
At around 30 hours I came across a distress signal which ended up being a giant trade ship being attacked by lots of smaller ships, I defeated them all and collected my reward. It was a fun break from foraging and hunting/scanning creatures and plants.
Combat while in your space craft is pretty simple, it's fairly fast paced and a really nice break from the majority of game play which is spent down on a planets surface, mining and foraging for resources.

The combat on foot is again, fairly simple. The enemies being a small variety of sentinels or alien creatures that are not so friendly. It would be great if we had a larger variety of sentinels to take on. So far I've seen three, a small floaty robo-eye thing, a mini-mech on all fours and a much taller, fairly huge, bi-pedal mech that can actual deal some damage if you're not prepared. (People making accusations that this huge sentinel is not in the game yet, can see my collection of NMS screen shots)


Things that I am not happy about/Do not like
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Alien creature AI and interaction
I watched all of the No Man's Sky E3 presentation footage. Most of us have, we all saw the scene with Triceratops-like alien crashing through the jungle, pushing trees out the way. This scene also has another more Brontosaurus-like alien bathing in some fairly shallow water.
Well, I've never seen anything nearly as cool as this, in terms of actual alien life/creatures OR in terms of the way the alien creatures AI works. (EDIT - Proof of awesome looking Brontosaurus-like aliens have been posted here - https://i.imgur.com/RP4HTI5.jpg)

Alien creatures don't seem to bathe, drink or eat in anyway, or do anything really. Some times they lay down and appear to be sleeping, that's about it. (EDIT - You can feed alien creatures, so I guess they do eat)
(EDIT - They DO hunt each other)
When you come across a more aggressive alien, it charges at you. I'm severely disappointed about this.

I haven't seen an alien creature do anything cool. Actually, you can feed some of them and they will sometimes dig up a rare mineral or item for you. So, sleeping or digging is about it for now. Again, even on the more widely alien creature inhabited planets, aliens are WAY more spaced out than the E3 game footage showed.

Multiplayer
♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mulitplayer, there I said it. We've all seen the 'Tell me lies, tell me sweat little lies' YouTube video. As someone that works in the game development industry I understand and appreciate that changes can and will happen during the development process. But for me and a lot of others, it's more about the lack of clarity and the vague answers that are getting us all rather miffed. Hello Games, Sean Murray, get your act together and put out a press release. Give us some facts on how exactly multiplayer works.

To sum it all up
A good friend of mine described NMS as a 'Create your own adventure' game, and I think that hits the nail on the head. The exploration, crafting, resource collection/management is awesome, but you need to have an imagination and be able to enjoy playing with patience.

If you go into No Man's Sky expecting hardcore survival mechanics or a story with the detail and depth of something like The Wicher 3, you'll be disappointed. This is for the most part, an exploration game. Let your imagination pave the way and just enjoy the sheer variety and vastness of the Universe and beyond.

Patches 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3 combined have made this game quite an addicting experience for me.  If you like open world, I mean really open world, combined with a sense of direction in the form of quests or missions (added by the recent patches), this game should easily give you 60+ hours of content.  The quests take you along nicely through the various things to do such as repairing and fueling your warp drive, getting started on your base, and adding components to it on a need-driven basis.  

If you like a challenge, survival mode pulls no puches (and permadeath is the same difficulty);  It is brutal.  It will kill you.  You will start on a planet that wants to eat you alive, and when you get off it and think you're over the hump, one wrong move such as being caught without the resource or fuel you need and you're dead.  You're going to give up and go back to Normal mode (I did) unless you're a boss.

The distractions are what give you (or me at least) zen-like moments-- scanning the flora and fauna around you; drifting serenely across the landscape in your ship, with a vague objective but mostly just taking in the view and losing track of time; walking along on foot from one resource or landmark to the next, while listening to the background music which creates a perfect blend of mystery, wonder, and calm.

Reviews.181829:
This was the first game I ever pre-ordered.
When I tell people that, they laugh.

No Man's Sky originally promised so much in the pre-release advertisements, it seemed too good to be true. From the day it was announced, it provoked my imagination to no end.
I remember talking about it with my skeptical friends, spiralling off to them about how incredible it would be to explore a life-sized universe in a custom spaceship, battling hordes of pirates and discovering countless incredible planets and claiming them as my own.

Needless to say, after all the hype and speculation, the release of the game will forever be remembered as one of the biggest letdowns in gaming history, and a testament to to risks of pre-ordering.
To call it "Early access" was insulting.
It was unrefined and buggy - an empty, uninspired, universe-sized beta-state game that had been sold with the pricetag of a bonafide title.
I'd go as far as to say it was almost a scam.

Unfortunately that hard truth only dawned on me after accidentally overstepping Steam's play limit, and I was subsequently refused the refund I'd requested.
I argued that over half of my "Play time" was spent waiting for the game to actually load, which was true. I also argued that the game was a cruel trick that had been seemingly deliberately mis-sold to the entire gaming community, and you only had to read an article on it or watch a YouTube review to understand the sheer gravity of the lie that was No Man's Sky. 
Steam didn't care. 
Two hours of open application = No refund.

I felt bitter towards the game after that.
Despite it admittedly being my own fault for not being careful and forfeiting any chance of a refund, I felt robbed by the entire platform.
I left No Man's Sky a damning negative review with a big red thumbs-down, stopped trying to play it altogether, and vowed never to pre-order a game again. 
Because I was also new to PC gaming at the time, I even considered switching back to console gaming.

---

Since then, however, I'm still a PC gamer.
Four years later, I knew the developers had taken accountability and actively responded to all the negative feedback, and I was hearing a lot of good things about the "New" No Man's Sky, so I opened it again and started properly learning how to play.

I was delighted to find the developers had taken full responsibility for the mess they'd first delivered.
They polished the game up, released tons of bug fixes, and gave us dozens of updates with new content to make the game more enjoyable.
They even made the game temporarily half price to attract new players and recover the refunded ones.
It was a genuine, honest turnaround and they deserve full credit for it.

Is it the game everyone wanted it to be?
No, of course not.
Yes, it was initially greatly exaggerated and oversold to the public.
No, you shouldn't expect it to be an incredible, overwhelming experience that will utterly blow your mind.
No Man's Sky is an indie game made by a relatively small developer.
Again, full credit to them, it's astonishingly better than when it was first released, and I'm sure it'd be fun to play in VR, but realistically, it will never be the game everyone imagined when it was first announced.

It's a large-scale sandbox game about piloting, exploring, mining, shooting, building, upgrading, potentially making a few online friends, and (Spoiler alert) eventually finishing the game and doing it all again.
If that's what you're into, you'll enjoy this game.
At the time of writing this, I've put over 100 hours into it, and I'm nowhere near finished with it.

No Man's Sky was released in 2016 and it's still relevant, frequently updated, with a large community following, even after such a bad launch. 
That in itself indicates a decent game.
If you're unsure about it, wait for a sale, it's often going for half price and well worth it.

---

Hello Games, if you're reading this; Thank you.
All is forgiven.

This game has really turned itself around.  I've been playing for a while now and find the game incredibly relaxing. There's an interesting narrative, beautiful visuals, intuitive base building mechanics, and a multitude of places to go and things to see. I see so many reviews complaining about "doing the same thing" and "getting bored 10 hours in" and I'm baffled. They must've just never tried to progress the story and just stayed in one area because here I am, almost 24 hours in and I feel like I'm only just scratching the surface. 
That being said, exploration and resource gathering/management is a big part of the game. If you don't enjoy that, or just get bored when you can't spend every second of your gaming experience in balls-to-the-wall combat, this game isn't for you. Additionally if you immediately want to just be a space tycoon buying vast quantities of goods to trade, you'll have to wait a while. This is a game meant to be enjoyed in slow, long sips. Taking your time and exploring, crafting, and making your way ever closer to that next goal. You don't get anywhere immediately. And I feel like that's where the magic happens.

It's fun alone, it's fun with friends, and its the perfect game to just sit back and relax while playing. Buy on sale or with a key since $60 is a little steep in terms of price. Buggy at times, but overall a wonderful experience that I can see myself continuing to enjoy.

NMS has a serious flaw in its inventory management system in that when you want to craft an item, instead of allowing you to craft it in the same slot as an ingredient, you must have a free slot just for the new item even though the ingredient will disappear once you have made it.  This means that you may have to get rid of something that you need for another recipe, slowing you down even more.  The reason that this is such a nuisance is that the inventory that you are given is already miniscule, however you can increase it through finding exosuit upgrades. I was very excited for this game's release and feel let down by the amount of content that was left out.  The space battles are cool except for having to manually repair your shields mid battle.  However, they are not as cool as was promised originally where the devs said that there would be warring factions that you could hop into massive battles on whichever faction's side you were on.  Instead, the most you get is some space pirates attacking 3 or 4 freighters.  The AI and alien species are extremely limited almost to the point where you feel like you are talking to the same characters over and over again.  You go in a building, there's the same looking guy sitting in a chair the same way as the last one was on the previous planet/space station.  Hopefully this game will eventually have the content that it needs to hold a 60 dollar price tag.  This price is far beyond what the game is worth.  Don't get me wrong, the game is a huge step in procedural generation technology.  However, a procedural gen tech demo is not enough to charge 60 bucks.  This game in its current state is worth about 20 dollars maximum.  The devs really needed to wait until the game was complete instead of rushing it out when the game wasn't ready.  Hopefully they don't do what other companies have tried in the past and release promised content as paid DLC in the future.

Edit: 2/18/2021 - I have changed my stance on this game, as the developers have been extremely hard at work listening to their community and fixing the issues that were present at launch.  I will support teams that put effort into redeeming themselves like this.  I now recommend this title.

[h1]Mind-Blowing Space Sandbox[/h1]

My mind was blown! I'm glad I hadn't been privy to all the pre-release hype because I avoided having my mind pre-blown.

[i]No Man's Sky[/i] bears the same innovative, technical wonder that accompanied the birth of the sandbox genre when [i]GTA3[/i] launched nearly 15 years ago (sans gratutitous bloodshed). The size of the game's universe is alarming and humbling. The permutations of landscapes, flora, and fauna is staggering. From the first moment to 40 hours later, I felt like I was on a true journey of discovery, lost, infinitesimally unimportant and surrounded by lands, creatures, worlds, and stars far greater and more vast than I could ever comprehend.

I like that!

I'm aware of the limitations associated with a procedurally-generated [strike]world[/strike] universe, and while they might sway some players, I find them thematically engaging. For instance, not every planet is teeming with herds of super-cool, dinosaur-like aliens. Some landscapes are icky enough to induce nausea. And I don't encounter white-knuckle dogfights every time I approach a space station. But that randomness is [i]exactly[/i] what makes this game a true journey. An exploration. An unplanned, unpredictable dive into beautiful--though often languid--chaos.

The changes team [b]Happy Games[/b] has made in the last year to improve and expand on the game's original features are impressive. They not only satisfied the trolls under the bridge, they fed them, and all the rest of us, so much new material, we've got things to do and places to go for years to come!

This is a TRUE sci-fi marvel and I don't regret a second I've spent exploring!

No Man's Sky is NOT for everyone as it marketed itself to be. It's boring, repetitive and can put you into existential crisis if you stare at its abyss deep enough. I also would never grab it at full price.
